ex.ko: 책을 읽기 시작하면 휴대폰을 덜 보게 돼요.

ex.note: 읽기 시작하다 is the fixed start-doing frame.

읽다.nuance: 읽다 has pronunciation changes, but beginners can first memorize 읽어요 as the practical polite form.
읽다.explanation: "to read" in Korean is 읽다 (ikda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 읽어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 읽다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 책을 읽어요 ("read a book.") — then reshape the same stem into 읽고 싶어요 (desire), 읽을 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 읽어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
읽다.shortExplanation: 읽다 means "to read" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 읽다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 읽어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 읽다 becomes 읽을 수 있어요 ("can") and 읽을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

examples.en: I read a book.

examples.en: Please read this sentence.

ex.ko: 예문을 듣는 게 단어 외우기에 도움이 돼요.
ex.en: Listening to example sentences helps with memorizing words.
ex.note: 듣는 게 presents listening as the concrete helpful action.

듣다.nuance: 듣다 is ㄷ irregular: 듣다 becomes 들어요 in polite speech.
듣다.explanation: 듣다 (deutda) means "to listen". Start from the polite form 들어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 듣다. A strong first sentence is 음악을 들어요 ("listen to music."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 듣다 also becomes 듣고 싶어요 (want), 들을 수 있어요 (can), and 못 들어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then bend it.
듣다.shortExplanation: 듣다 means "to listen" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 듣다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 들어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
듣다 changes to 들어요, not 듣어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem: ㄷ → ㄹ
conjugationTips.body: 듣다 is a ㄷ-irregular verb. The final ㄷ becomes ㄹ before a vowel ending, so it conjugates to 들어요, never the literal ㄷ + 어요. The ㄷ stays ㄷ before a consonant ending (듣고, 듣습니다).

말하다.nuance: Use 로 for language: 한국어로 말해요, 영어로 말해요. 말하다 can mean both “speak” and “say,” so the object or quote decides the English translation.
말하다.explanation: "to speak / say" in Korean is 말하다 (malhada). cluster.title: 말하다 vs 이야기하다
cluster.rule: Use 말하다 for producing words — saying one thing, or speaking a language. Use 이야기하다 when there's a back-and-forth or a story being told: chatting with someone, usually marked with 와/과 or 하고.

ex.en: For this issue, the reason is the most important thing.
ex.note: 문제는 sets the frame; 이유가 is the key subject.

문제.nuance: 문제(問題, 'ask + topic') has two everyday senses English keeps apart: a trouble or difficulty ('we have a problem') AND a question on a test or exercise ('problem 3'). Crucially, both are solved with the same verb 풀다 (literally 'to untie/loosen') — 문제를 풀다 works for a math item and for a real-life difficulty alike, where English would switch to 'answer' vs 'solve.' Other key partners: 문제가 생기다 (a problem arises), 문제가 되다 (to become an issue), and the handy one-word 문제없어요 ('no problem'). Contrast 문제 with 질문 (a question you ASK someone to get information) — a test 문제 is a problem to solve, but raising your hand to ask is 질문하다, not 문제하다. The English-speaker pitfall is the subject/object split: existence and arising take 이 (문제가 있다/생기다), but solving takes 를 (문제를 풀다) — learners often say 문제가 풀어요.
문제.explanation: 문제 (munje) = "problem". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 문제가 있어요 ("there is a problem") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 문제, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
문제.shortExplanation: 문제 means "problem" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 문제가 풀어요. Solving is transitive — the problem is the object → 문제를 풀어요.
Using 문제 for a question you ask. To ask someone something is 질문(을) 하다; 문제 is a problem/test item, not an inquiry.
Saying 문제를 있어요. 있다 marks existence with the subject — it must be 문제가 있어요.

usagePhrases.note: 생기다 = come into being; subject 이

examples.en: There's one small problem here.
examples.note: Simple: 문제가 있다 — a problem exists (subject 이).

examples.en: I solved all the math problems.
examples.note: Everyday: 문제를 풀다 also covers test questions; object 를.

examples.en: That's not a problem at all.
examples.note: Real situation: 문제가 되다 / 안 되다 = (not) become an issue.

ex.ko: 공부하기 전에 오늘 목표를 먼저 써요.
ex.en: Before studying, I write today's goal first.
ex.note: 기 전에 is the natural before-doing frame.

공부하다.nuance: 공부하다 is noun + 하다, so the short negative is often 공부 안 해요.
공부하다.explanation: 공부하다 (gongbuhada) = "to study". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 공부해요 plus one useful sentence like 한국어를 공부해요 ("study Korean."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 공부하고 싶어요 for what you want, 공부할 수 있어요 for what you can, 공부 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help.
공부하다.shortExplanation: 공부하다 means "to study" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 공부하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 공부해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 공부하다 becomes 공부할 수 있어요 ("can") and 공부할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

보다.nuance: 보다 covers seeing, watching, and looking at something. Context tells which English verb fits.
보다.explanation: "to see / watch" in Korean is 보다 (boda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 봐요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 보다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 영화를 봐요 ("watch a movie.") — then reshape the same stem into 보고 싶어요 (desire), 볼 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 봐요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
보다.shortExplanation: 보다 means "to see / watch" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 보다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 봐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 보다 becomes 볼 수 있어요 ("can") and 볼 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

cluster.title: 만나다 vs 보다
cluster.rule: 만나다 is the neutral "meet" and is never wrong. But in real casual speech Koreans constantly use 보다 with a person — 내일 봐요, 친구 봤어요 — so 보다 means "see / hang out with" someone you already know, while 만나다 fits arranged or first-time meetings.

쉬다.en: to rest, to take a break

ex.ko: 이틀 푹 쉬었더니 몸이 훨씬 가벼워졌어요.

ex.note: A discovery about what worked — exactly what -았/었더니 is for.

쉬다.nuance: 쉬다 is used for taking a break, resting, or being off work/school.
쉬다.explanation: "to rest" in Korean is 쉬다 (swida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 쉬어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 쉬다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 좀 쉬어요 ("rest a little.") — then reshape the same stem into 쉬고 싶어요 (desire), 쉴 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 쉬어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

ex.ko: 지훈이는 요즘 프로젝트 때문에 진짜 바쁘대요.
ex.en: They say Jihoon is really busy these days because of a project.
ex.note: An adjective, so -대요 attaches bare: 바쁘대요, never 바쁜대요.

바쁘다.nuance: 바쁘다 becomes 바빠요 in polite speech. It is a high-frequency reason word because 바빠서 못 가요 politely explains why a plan is impossible.
바쁘다.explanation: "to be busy" is 바쁘다 (bappeuda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 바빠요 ("I am busy."). Watch the particle attached to 바쁘다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.
바쁘다.shortExplanation: 바쁘다 means "to be busy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
바쁘다 becomes 바빠요, not 바쁘어요.

conjugationTips.title: Describing a noun: ㄴ/은 vs ㄹ/을
conjugationTips.body: To put 바쁘다 in front of a noun, use the ㄴ/은 form for how something is right now: 바쁜 것 ("a busy thing"). The ㄹ/을 form points to something that will or might become that way later. So 뜨거운 물 is water that is hot now, but 뜨거울 물 is water that will be hot — same adjective, different time feeling. For everyday description, reach for the ㄴ/은 form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem: ㅡ drop
conjugationTips.body: 바쁘다 loses its ㅡ vowel before 아/어, giving 바빠요 (the same drop turns 바쁘다 into 바빠요). The ㅡ never takes its own 어요, so don't add 어요 to the bare ㅡ.

usagePhrases.en: I am busy, so I cannot go.

examples.en: I am busy today.
examples.note: Topic.

examples.en: I am busy, so I cannot go.

앉다.nuance: 앉아 주세요 is a polite request; 앉으세요 is also common and a little more direct.
앉다.explanation: 앉다 (anjda) means "to sit". Start from the polite form 앉아요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 앉다. A strong first sentence is 여기 앉아요 ("sit here."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 앉다 also becomes 앉고 싶어요 (want), 앉을 수 있어요 (can), and 못 앉아요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
앉다.shortExplanation: 앉다 means "to sit" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 앉다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 앉아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 앉다 becomes 앉을 수 있어요 ("can") and 앉을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

examples.en: May I sit here?
examples.note: Permission.

examples.en: Please sit for a moment.
examples.note: Request.

examples.en: I cannot sit on the floor.

ex.en: Don't act clueless when you know perfectly well.
ex.note: 모르는 척하다 also means deliberately ignoring somebody you recognise.

모르다.nuance: 모르다 is the standalone verb 'to not know / be unaware of', the lexical opposite of 알다, and it likewise takes the object marker 을/를: 길을 몰라요. It is a 르-irregular: when an 아/어 ending attaches, the 르 stem doubles the ㄹ and the vowel drops, so 모르 + 아요 → 몰라요 (never 모르아요) and the past is 몰랐어요. The crucial register tool is 겠: 잘 모르겠어요 ('I'm not quite sure') is markedly softer and more natural than a blunt 몰라요, which can sound curt or even dismissive depending on tone, so Koreans lean on the 겠 form constantly when admitting ignorance politely. Compare 모르다 with 헷갈리다 ('to be confused / mix things up'): 모르다 is having no information at all, while 헷갈리다 is having information but getting it tangled. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation — applying a regular pattern to get 모르아요 instead of the irregular 몰라요 — and forgetting that the smooth, courteous version is 잘 모르겠어요.
모르다.explanation: 모르다 (moreuda) = "to not know". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 몰라요 plus one useful sentence like 길을 몰라요 ("I don't know the way"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 모르고 싶어요 for what you want, 모를 수 있어요 for what you can, 알아요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
모르다.shortExplanation: 모르다 means "to not know" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 모르다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 몰라요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Conjugating it regularly as 모르아요 — 모르다 is a 르-irregular, so 모르 + 아요 becomes 몰라요 (past 몰랐어요).
Blurting a bare 몰라요 when asked something — it can sound curt; soften with 잘 모르겠어요 to stay polite.
Using 모르다 when you mean you mixed two things up — that is 헷갈리다 (e.g. 이름이 헷갈려요 'I keep confusing the names'), not 몰라요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 모르다 becomes 모를 수 있어요 ("can") and 모를 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 모르다 has an irregular stem (르 irregular). Memorize its polite form 몰라요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

usagePhrases.note: the thing not known takes 을/를, like 알다

examples.en: Sorry, I don't really know the way.
examples.note: polite apology + 잘 몰라요 to be gentle

examples.en: I didn't know that person's name.
examples.note: past 몰랐어요 from the 르-irregular stem

examples.ko: 글쎄요, 저도 잘 모르겠어요. 같이 찾아볼까요?

examples.en: Hmm, I'm not sure either. Shall we look it up together?

ex.en: I decided to start with walking first.
ex.note: 걷기 names the activity; 시작하기로 했어요 reports the decision.

걷다.nuance: 걷다 means to walk on foot and is a ㄷ irregular verb: before a vowel ending the final ㄷ softens to ㄹ, so the 요-form is 걸어요 (not 걷어요) and the past is 걸었어요. Before a consonant ending the ㄷ stays put, so the formal form remains 걷습니다 and you say 걷지 마세요, 걷고 싶어요. The nearest relative is 산책하다 ('take a stroll'): 걷다 is the raw act of walking anywhere, while 산책하다 implies a leisurely walk for pleasure, so 'I walk to work' is 걸어서 출근해요, never 산책해서 출근해요. The trap for English speakers is that 걷다 doesn't take an object the way 'walk the dog' does — Korean uses 산책시키다 for that, and the path you walk takes 을/를 (공원을 걸어요), so don't reach for 에. Also remember 걸어서 ('on foot') is one fixed chunk for describing how you travel.
걷다.explanation: 걷다 (geotda) means "to walk". Start from the polite form 걸어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 걷다. A strong first sentence is 공원을 걸어요 ("I walk in/through the park"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 걷다 also becomes 걷고 싶어요 (want), 걸을 수 있어요 (can), and 못 걸어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
걷다.shortExplanation: 걷다 means "to walk" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 걷다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 걸어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Keeping the ㄷ and saying 걷어요/걷었어요 — because 걷다 is a ㄷ irregular, the ㄷ becomes ㄹ before vowels, so the correct forms are 걸어요/걸었어요 (the ㄷ only survives before consonants, as in 걷습니다).
Saying 공원에 걸어요 to mean 'I walk in the park' — the space you walk through is the path/object and takes 을/를, so it must be 공원을 걸어요; 에 would wrongly mark a destination.
Translating 'walk the dog' literally as 개를 걸어요 — 걷다 can't take a creature as its object that way; Korean says 개를 산책시켜요 ('make the dog stroll').

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 걷다 becomes 걸을 수 있어요 ("can") and 걸을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem: ㄷ → ㄹ
conjugationTips.body: 걷다 is a ㄷ-irregular verb. The final ㄷ becomes ㄹ before a vowel ending, so it conjugates to 걸어요, never the literal ㄷ + 어요. The ㄷ stays ㄷ before a consonant ending (듣고, 듣습니다).

usagePhrases.note: the route or space you cover takes 을/를, not 에

examples.en: I walk in the park every day.
examples.note: 걷다 is intransitive but the park you traverse takes 을 as the path

examples.en: It takes ten minutes on foot to the station.
examples.note: 걸어서 'on foot' is the everyday answer to how you get somewhere

examples.ko: 다리를 다쳐서 지금은 잘 못 걸어요.
examples.romanization: darireul dachyeoseo jigeumeun jal mot georeoyo.
examples.en: I hurt my leg, so I can't walk well right now.
examples.note: 못 걸어요 uses the ㄷ→ㄹ vowel form; 못 걷어요 is wrong

걸리다.en: to be hung; to get caught; to take (time)

ex.ko: 저 그림은 작년부터 저 벽에 걸려 있어요.
ex.en: That painting has been hanging on that wall since last year.
ex.note: 걸다 → 걸리다. The same verb also gives 감기에 걸리다 and 시간이 걸리다.

걸리다.nuance: 걸리다 is a high-frequency verb that fans out into three everyday senses learners meet fast: (1) time being needed — 시간이 걸리다; (2) catching an illness — 감기에 걸리다; and (3) getting caught/busted — 경찰한테 걸리다, 거짓말이 걸리다. The thread linking them is its origin as the passive of 걸다 ('to hang/hook'): something gets hooked — by time, by sickness, by the law — so 벽에 그림이 걸려 있어요 ('a picture is hung on the wall') is the same word. The number-one English-speaker pitfall is the subject/particle: for 'take time' the *time* is the subject (시간이 걸려요), never 시간을 걸려요; and for illness you must use 에 (감기에 걸리다), not the object 를. Compare 걸리다 ('take/require time') with 들다, which is used for cost/effort/money (돈이 들다) — 시간이 걸리다 vs 돈이 들다 is a pairing Koreans keep distinct. It is a regular ㅣ-stem verb: 걸리 + 어 contracts to 걸려요.
걸리다.explanation: 걸리다 (geollida) means "to take (time) / to get caught". Start from the polite form 걸려요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 걸리다. A strong first sentence is 시간이 얼마나 걸려요? ("How long does it take?"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 걸리다 also becomes 걸리고 싶어요 (want), 걸릴 수 있어요 (can), and 걸릴 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
걸리다.shortExplanation: 걸리다 means "to take (time) / to get caught" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 걸리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 걸려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
For 'how long does it take', the time is the subject: 시간이 얼마나 걸려요?, never 시간을 걸려요.
To catch a cold, use the particle 에 (감기에 걸리다), not 를 — 감기를 걸렸어요 is wrong.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 걸리다 becomes 걸릴 수 있어요 ("can") and 걸릴 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not take (time) / to get caught.
I want to take (time) / to get caught.
I can take (time) / to get caught.
I have to take (time) / to get caught.

usagePhrases.note: 걸리다 with 시간 is THE way to ask about duration; the time, not you, is the subject.

examples.en: It takes an hour to get home
examples.note: Travel time: the duration is the subject — 한 시간이 걸려요.

examples.en: I caught a cold again
examples.note: A fixed expression every beginner needs; note the 에 particle.

examples.en: I was speeding and got caught by the police
examples.note: The 'get busted' sense, with the catcher marked by 한테.

ex.ko: 제시간에 도착했더라면 면접을 볼 수 있었을 거예요.
ex.en: If I had arrived on time, I could have had the interview.
ex.note: 도착했더라면 is useful for exams, interviews, trains, and appointments.

도착하다.nuance: 도착하다 is Sino-Korean 到着(도착: 到 reach + 着 attach/touch down) plus 하다 — the moment of REACHING and touching a destination. Its mirror is 출발하다(depart), and the key is the particle: you arrive AT a place with 에 (호텔에 도착해요), whereas 출발하다 leaves FROM a place with 에서. Don't confuse it with 들어가다/들어오다(enter): 도착하다 is reaching the destination's threshold, not stepping inside a building. As a 하다 verb, 하 + 아 fuses to 해 (도착해요) and the short negative and inability split the noun off: 도착 안 해요, 도착 못 해요. The classic English-speaker error is copying 'arrive at' as 에서 — 'at' here is the static endpoint 에, so 공항에 도착해요, and 공항에서 도착해요 is wrong.
도착하다.explanation: 도착하다 (dochakada) = "to arrive". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 도착해요 plus one useful sentence like 공항에 도착해요 ("I arrive at the airport."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 도착하고 싶어요 for what you want, 도착할 수 있어요 for what you can, 도착 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help.
도착하다.shortExplanation: 도착하다 means "to arrive" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 도착하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 도착해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 에서 for the arrival point (공항에서 도착했어요) by mapping English 'arrive at'. The destination reached takes 에; 에서 marks a source, which belongs to 출발/떠나다.
Mixing it up with 들어가다 (enter) — 도착하다 means you've reached the place, not that you've walked inside. To go in through the door, use 들어가다.
Forming inability as 못 도착해요 in this set — the natural split-negative for the 하다 verb is 도착 못 해요, keeping 못 right before 해요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 도착하다 becomes 도착할 수 있어요 ("can") and 도착할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Arrival point takes 에, never 에서

examples.en: I just got to the station.
examples.note: Arrival point 역 takes 에; 도착 + 하 + 았 → 도착했어요.

examples.en: Call me once you arrive at the station.
examples.note: 면 = when/once; 주세요 makes it a polite request.

examples.ko: 길이 막혀서 제시간에 도착 못 해요.
examples.romanization: giri makyeoseo jesigane dochang mo taeyo.
examples.en: Traffic's bad, so I can't make it on time.
examples.note: Inability splits as 도착 못 해요 around the noun.

ex.ko: 여기까지 왔는데 지금 포기해 버리면 너무 아깝잖아요.
ex.en: It'd be such a waste to just give up now after coming this far.
ex.note: -아/어 버리다 makes giving up sound abrupt and final.

포기하다.nuance: 포기하다 = to give up, abandon, or relinquish a goal, plan, claim, or even a person. The hanja 抛棄 is vivid: 抛 'to throw/hurl away' + 棄 'to discard, abandon', so the image is hurling something aside and walking off — a decisive letting-go, not a gentle fade. Contrast 포기하다 (stop pursuing a goal entirely) with 그만두다 (stop/quit an ongoing activity — a job, a habit) and with 단념하다 (a more bookish 'resign oneself to abandoning hope'); in speech 포기하다 is the everyday choice. Grammar: it pairs with 을/를 (목표를 포기하다) or with 는 거 / 는 걸 (사는 걸 포기하다 = 'give up on buying'). Culturally the word is loaded: N포세대, the 'give-up generation', names young Koreans said to have surrendered dating, marriage, and kids to economic pressure. English-speaker pitfall: the negative is 포기 안 해 / 포기 못 해 (noun + 안/못 + 해), NOT 안 포기해.
포기하다.explanation: 포기하다 (pogihada) = "to give up". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 포기해요 plus one useful sentence like 포기하지 마 ("Don't give up"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 포기하고 싶어 for what you want, 포기할 수 있어 for what you can, 포기 못 해 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
포기하다.shortExplanation: 포기하다 means "to give up" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 포기하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 포기해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Spacing the negative wrong — it's 포기 안 해 / 포기 못 해 (noun + 안/못 + 해), not 안 포기해.
Saying 일을 포기했어 to mean 'I quit my job' — for quitting an activity/job use 그만뒀어 (그만두다); 포기하다 is for giving up on a goal or outcome.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 포기하다 becomes 포기할 수 있어 ("can") and 포기할 거야 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: The standard motivational line — friends, coaches, dramas all use it.

examples.en: I gave up on the diet ages ago.
examples.note: 진작에 = 'long ago / already'; 다이어트 포기 is a relatable running joke.

examples.ko: 집값 보고 서울에 집 사는 건 포기했어.
examples.romanization: jipgaps bogo seoure jip saneun geon pogihaesseo.
examples.en: After seeing the prices, I gave up on buying a place in Seoul.
examples.note: 집값 = housing prices; ~는 건 포기하다 = 'give up on doing'. A very real 20-30s concern.

examples.ko: 여기까지 왔는데 지금 포기하기엔 너무 아까워.
examples.romanization: yeogikkaji wanneunde jigeum pogihagien neomu akkawo.
examples.en: We've come this far — it'd be a waste to give up now.
examples.note: 아깝다 = 'too good to waste'; 여기까지 왔는데 = 'having come this far'.

ex.ko: 하마터면 여권을 두고 공항에 갈 뻔했어요.
ex.en: I very nearly went to the airport without my passport.
ex.note: 하마터면 almost always goes first and demands -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 at the end.

하마터면.nuance: 하마터면 is dramatic but natural when the speaker feels relieved that the event did not happen.
하마터면.explanation: 하마터면 (hamateomyeon) = "almost / by a narrow margin". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 하마터면 울 뻔했어요. ("I almost cried.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 하마터면, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
하마터면.shortExplanation: 하마터면 means "almost / by a narrow margin" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 하마터면 alone; pair it with -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요.

usagePhrases.note: 하마터면 adds the near-miss alarm feeling.

examples.en: I almost lost my wallet.
examples.note: A common everyday close-call sentence.

ex.en: A typhoon came in, so the flight was cancelled.
ex.note: 취소되다 is itself a passive, which is why nobody is blamed for the cancellation.

취소되다.nuance: 취소되다 is the passive/intransitive side of 취소하다. The event, appointment, order, or reservation that no longer happens becomes the subject with 이/가: 행사가 취소됐어요, 예약이 취소됐어요. If a person actively cancels something, use 을/를 + 취소하다: 제가 예약을 취소했어요. Do not confuse cancellation with postponement: 연기되다 means it will happen later, while 취소되다 means the plan is no longer going ahead. 변경되다 means details changed but the event may still happen.
취소되다.explanation: 취소되다 (chwisodoeda) means "to be canceled." Use N이/가 취소되다 for the canceled event, and N을/를 취소하다 when someone actively cancels it.
취소되다.shortExplanation: 취소되다 is passive: the canceled plan takes 이/가; the person who cancels uses 취소하다 with 을/를.
commonMistakes: Saying 행사를 취소됐어요. Passive 취소되다 needs a subject: 행사가 취소됐어요.
Using 취소되다 when the event is merely moved to a later date. That is 연기되다.
Writing 취소됬어요. The correct spelling is 취소됐어요, from 되어 → 돼.
Mixing active and passive roles: 제가 취소됐어요 normally means ‘I was canceled,’ not ‘I canceled it.’ Say 제가 예약을 취소했어요.

conjugationTips.title: 되다 → 돼요
conjugationTips.body: 취소되다 contracts in speech and writing: 취소돼요, 취소됐어요, 취소될 거예요. Keep 되어/돼 straight: 취소되어요 contracts to 취소돼요.

usagePhrases.note: The canceled plan is the subject.
Active 취소하다 takes the object 를.
취소된 is the completed modifier form.

examples.ko: 비 때문에 야외 공연이 갑자기 취소됐어요.
examples.romanization: bi ttaemune yaoe gongyeoni gapjagi chwisodwaesseoyo.
examples.en: The outdoor performance was suddenly canceled because of the rain.
examples.note: The performance is the subject of the passive verb.

examples.ko: 수업은 취소된 게 아니라 다음 주로 연기됐어요.
examples.romanization: sueobeun chwisodoen ge anira daeum juro yeongidwaesseoyo.
examples.en: The class was not canceled; it was postponed until next week.
examples.note: Directly contrasts cancellation and postponement.

examples.ko: 제가 예약을 취소했는데 환불은 아직 처리되지 않았어요.
examples.romanization: jega yeyageul chwisohanneunde hwanbureun ajik cheoridoeji anasseoyo.
examples.en: I canceled the reservation, but the refund has not been processed yet.
examples.note: Active cancellation by the speaker, followed by another passive process.

ex.ko: 친구랑 노느라고 숙제를 하나도 못 했어요.
ex.en: I was messing around with a friend, so I didn't do any of my homework.
ex.note: 놀다 loses its ㄹ before -느라고, giving 노느라고.

숙제.nuance: 숙제 is Sino-Korean 宿題 — 宿 'lodging/stay overnight' + 題 'topic/problem', literally a 'problem to take home overnight', i.e. work a teacher assigns to be done outside class. The verb is locked: Koreans say 숙제를 하다 'do homework', and 숙제를 내다 means a student turns it in (while a teacher 내다 a 숙제 means 'assign/set' it — context decides). Contrast 숙제 with 공부(工夫, 'study') and 과제(課題, 'assignment/coursework'): 공부하다 is the broad act of studying anything, whereas 숙제 is a specific assigned task, and 과제 is the more formal university word for a project or paper. The big English-speaker pitfall is translating 'do my homework' as 숙제를 만들다 'make homework' (✗ — that sounds like you created the assignment) or 숙제를 공부하다 (✗); the only natural pairing is 숙제를 하다.
숙제.explanation: "homework" is 숙제 (sukje). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 숙제를 하다 ("do homework"). Watch the particle attached to 숙제 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.
숙제.shortExplanation: 숙제 means "homework" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 숙제를 만들다 ('make homework') instead of 숙제를 하다 — 만들다 means create the task itself, not complete it.
Using 숙제를 공부하다 ✗. 공부하다 is general study; the set phrase to complete assigned work is 숙제를 하다.
Treating 숙제 as countable English plural and dropping the particle. You still need 를: 숙제를 했어요, not 숙제 했어요 in writing/formal speech.

usagePhrases.note: The fixed verb is 하다, never 만들다; object takes 를
많다 = many/much; the amount is the subject, so 가
내다 = submit/turn in (also 제출하다, more formal)
Noun-noun compound; 숙제 takes the subject as a modifier

examples.en: Did you finish all your homework?
examples.note: Casual question; 다 = 'all/completely', a very common collocation with 하다

examples.en: Today there isn't much homework.
examples.note: 별로 + negative = 'not really/not much'; amount is the subject (가)

examples.en: I forgot the homework and didn't bring it.
examples.note: 깜빡하다 = 'absent-mindedly forget', the natural verb students use

ex.en: Before starting exercise, I set a goal.
ex.note: 운동 is already a noun, so it can take 을 before 시작하다.

운동.nuance: 운동 is Sino-Korean, 運動 ('move-motion'), and is the umbrella word for physical exercise; it normally appears as 운동하다 (운동을 해요). Crucially it is NOT counted or pluralized like English 'a workout' — you don't say 운동들 for several sessions; you say 운동을 자주 해요. The nearest relative is 스포츠 (a borrowed word for organized sports as a category, e.g. watching 스포츠 on TV), whereas 운동 is the act of exercising your own body, so '운동선수' = athlete but '스포츠 경기' = a sports match. The very same 運動 also means a social 'movement/campaign' (민주화 운동 the democracy movement), so context decides. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 만들다 ('make') by analogy with 'make exercise' — Korean uses the light verb 하다; and remember the desire ending goes on the verb (운동하고 싶어요), never on the bare noun.
운동.explanation: 운동 (undong) means "exercise". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 운동을 해요 ("I exercise"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 운동 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
운동.shortExplanation: 운동 means "exercise" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 운동을 만들어요 by translating 'do/make exercise' literally — 만들다 means physically craft something; the correct light verb is 하다, so 운동을 해요.
Attaching the want-ending to the noun as 운동 싶어요 — -고 싶다 only fastens to a verb stem, so it must be 운동하고 싶어요 / 운동을 하고 싶어요.
Using 운동들 to mean several workouts — 운동 is non-count here; say 운동을 여러 번 해요 or 자주 운동해요 instead.

usagePhrases.note: 운동 takes the object marker 을 because 하다 acts on it
subject marker 이 after a consonant
-고 싶어요 attaches to the verb 하-, not to the noun
좋아하다 is a verb 'to like', so its object takes 을/를

examples.en: I exercise every day.
examples.note: the everyday 운동하다 frame for a habit

examples.en: I started exercising lately to lose weight.
examples.note: 운동을 시작하다 = take up working out

examples.ko: 헬스장에서 한 시간 동안 운동했더니 온몸이 뻐근해요.
examples.romanization: helseujangeseo han sigan dongan undonghaetdeoni onmomi ppeogeunhaeyo.
examples.en: After working out at the gym for an hour, my whole body is stiff.
examples.note: real gym talk; 운동하다 contracted, with a result

ex.ko: 그 버스를 탔더라면 약속 시간에 맞췄을 거예요.
ex.en: If I had taken that bus, I would have made it on time for the appointment.
ex.note: Transport words make counterfactuals concrete: take it, miss it, arrive late.

버스.nuance: 버스 is useful with 타다, 기다리다, 내리다, and 로/으로 for transportation method.
버스.explanation: 버스 (beoseu) = "bus". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 버스를 타요 ("I take the bus.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 버스, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.
버스.shortExplanation: 버스 means "bus" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 버스에 타요 as your first pattern; 버스를 타요 is the beginner frame.

examples.en: I take the bus.
examples.note: Transportation.

examples.en: I wait for the bus.
examples.note: Waiting.

examples.en: I get off at the next stop.
examples.note: Travel.

ex.en: I would have gone together with you.
ex.note: 같이 makes the regret relational, not just logistical.

같이.nuance: 같이 can mean together or like/as in other contexts; here it means together.
같이.explanation: 같이 (gachi) = "together". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 같이 가요 ("Let us go together.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 같이, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
같이.shortExplanation: 같이 means "together" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
For “with a friend,” say 친구하고/친구랑 같이, not 친구로 같이.

usagePhrases.en: I go together with a friend.

examples.en: Shall we go together?
examples.note: Suggestion.

examples.en: I study together with a friend.
examples.note: Together.

examples.en: I am going together too.
examples.note: Also.

cluster.title: 같이 vs 함께
cluster.rule: They mean the same thing and are almost always swappable; 같이 is what people actually say out loud every day, while 함께 sounds a bit warmer and more polished, so it turns up in writing, invitations and slogans.

members.hint: the one you actually say out loud
same meaning, a bit more polished

example.en: It's even better if we go together.

ex.ko: 안경을 쓰니까 칠판 글씨가 훨씬 잘 보여요.
ex.en: With my glasses on I can see the writing on the board much better.
ex.note: With 이/가 and no object it is the passive of 보다.

보이다.nuance: 보이다 is the passive/spontaneous counterpart of 보다 (to look): something enters your field of vision on its own, so the thing seen takes 이/가 (산이 보여요 = 'the mountain is visible'), NOT 을/를. The 요-form contracts 보이-+-어요 → 보여요 (past 보였어요). The sharp contrast learners need is 보이다 vs 보다: 보다 is an active choice ('I look at / watch'), 보이다 is involuntary ('it is seen / comes into view'). A second, very frequent meaning is 'to look/seem' — adjective stem + 보이다 (행복해 보여요 'you look happy'; 비싸 보여요 'it looks expensive'); here English 'looks' maps cleanly. With 주다 it flips to active 'show' (보여 주다). The English-speaker pitfall: saying 산을 보여요 to mean 'I see the mountain' — that is wrong; use 산이 보여요 (it is visible) or 산을 봐요 (I look at it).
보이다.explanation: 보이다 (boi-da) means "to be seen". Start from the polite form 보여요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 보이다. A strong first sentence is 잘 보이다 ("to be clearly visible"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 보이다 also becomes 보이고 싶어요 (want), 보일 수 있어요 (can), and 못 보여요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
보이다.shortExplanation: 보이다 means "to be seen" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 보이다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 보여요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the seen thing with 을/를: 글씨를 안 보여요 is wrong. Because 보이다 is intransitive, say 글씨가 안 보여요 ('the letters aren't visible').
Confusing 보이다 with 보다. 'I can see it' for involuntary vision is 보여요, but 'I look at it / watch it' is 봐요 — don't use 보여요 for deliberate watching.
Forgetting the 'looks like' meaning. 'You look tired' is 피곤해 보여요, not 피곤한 것을 봐요 — adjective stem + 보이다 carries the 'seems' sense.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 보이다 becomes 보일 수 있어요 ("can") and 보일 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: 잘 (well) is the habitual partner for visibility; opposite is 안 보이다.

examples.en: The sea is very visible from here.
examples.note: The thing seen takes 이/가 (바다가), not 을/를 — this is intransitive.

examples.en: Please show me your ticket.
examples.note: 보여 주다 = 'show'; here it IS transitive because of 주다, so 표를 takes 를.

examples.en: You look tired. Get some rest.
examples.note: Adjective stem 피곤하- + 보여요 = 'looks ~', a hugely common everyday use.

ex.en: The question was easy, but the answer was difficult.
ex.note: 쉬웠는데 sets up contrast.

쉽다.nuance: 쉽다 is ㅂ irregular: 쉬워요, 쉬운. It helps learners talk about difficulty level, but the opposite 어렵다 is often needed in the same lesson.
쉽다.explanation: 쉽다 (swipda) = "to be easy". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 쉬워요 ("It is easy.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 쉽다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.
쉽다.shortExplanation: 쉽다 means "to be easy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
쉽다 becomes 쉬워요, not 쉽어요.

conjugationTips.title: Describing a noun: ㄴ/은 vs ㄹ/을
conjugationTips.body: To put 쉽다 in front of a noun, use the ㄴ/은 form for how something is right now: 쉬운 것 ("a easy thing"). The ㄹ/을 form points to something that will or might become that way later. So 뜨거운 물 is water that is hot now, but 뜨거울 물 is water that will be hot — same adjective, different time feeling. For everyday description, reach for the ㄴ/은 form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem: ㅂ → 우
conjugationTips.body: 쉽다 is a ㅂ-irregular word. Before a vowel ending the final ㅂ turns into 우, so the polite form is 쉬워요 — not a literal ㅂ + 어요. The same change gives the noun-describing form (맵다 → 매운, 쉽다 → 쉬운). Anchor on 쉬워요 and build the rest from it.

examples.en: This problem is easy.
examples.note: Topic.

examples.en: Korean is not easy.
examples.note: Careful negative.

examples.en: It is an easy sentence.
examples.note: Before noun.

ex.en: I think this method might be possible.
ex.note: Linked to dictionary card word-ext-1255.

가능하다.nuance: 가능하다 (可能, 可 'can/permissible' + 能 'ability') means 'possible / doable / available', and it is wonderfully practical for daily service questions — 예약 가능해요? ('Is a reservation possible?'), 카드 가능해요? ('Can I pay by card?'). In these, a noun sits directly before it and it neatly replaces a longer '-ㄹ 수 있다' clause, sounding crisp and businesslike. The softener 가능하면 ('if possible') makes requests polite, and the fixed frame 가능한 한 + adjective/adverb means 'as ~ as possible' (가능한 한 빨리 'as soon as possible') — note this is different from 가능한 N ('a possible N'). Its antonym is 불가능하다. One pitfall: while 가능하다 and '-ㄹ 수 있다' both render English 'can', '-ㄹ 수 있다' attaches to a verb stem describing an action you're able to do (갈 수 있어요 'I can go'), whereas 가능하다 attaches to a noun or stands alone judging feasibility — don't merge them into 갈 가능해요.
가능하다.explanation: 가능하다 (ganeunghada) = "to be possible". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: N 가능하다 ("N is possible / available") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 가능하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
가능하다.shortExplanation: 가능하다 means "to be possible" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 가능하다 (possible) with its 불- prefixed antonym 불가능하다 (impossible).
Mixing 가능한 N ('a possible N') with the 'as ~ as possible' meaning — for the latter the set form is 가능한 한 + adjective/adverb (가능한 한 천천히 'as slowly as possible').
Gluing 가능하다 onto a verb like '갈 가능해요' — to express ability with a verb use '-ㄹ 수 있다' (갈 수 있어요); 가능하다 follows a noun or stands alone.

usagePhrases.note: drops 이/가 in shop talk, e.g. 예약 가능해요?
set frame, e.g. 가능한 한 빨리 'as soon as possible'
the noun derived from the same 가능 root

examples.en: Is delivery possible today?
examples.note: asking at a shop; 배달 가능해요? is a fixed service phrase

examples.en: A refund is possible.
examples.note: 환불 = refund; the noun stands directly before 가능하다

examples.ko: 가능하면 회의를 오전으로 옮길 수 있을까요?
examples.romanization: ganeunghamyeon hoeuireul ojeoneuro olmgil su isseulkkayo?
examples.en: If possible, could we move the meeting to the morning?
examples.note: real polite request; 가능하면 cushions the ask

ex.ko: 메시지는 자주 보내지만 전화는 잘 안 해요.
ex.en: I send messages often, but I do not call much.
ex.note: 은/는 makes the contrast visible.

메시지.nuance: 메시지 is the loanword from English 'message' and covers chat/app messages broadly (a KakaoTalk message, a DM); the everyday near-synonym 문자 (literally 文字 'letters/characters') specifically means an SMS text, so '문자 보내' = 'text me' while '메시지' is the wider term. There's also 카톡, the verb-able brand shorthand for a KakaoTalk message, used constantly in real life (카톡 보낼게 'I'll Kakao you'). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, the recipient is marked with 한테/에게 ('to a person'), not the English bare object — 친구한테 메시지를 보내다, where 친구한테 = 'to my friend' and 메시지를 is the thing sent; second, the message arriving uses intransitive 오다 with 이/가 (메시지가 오다), but you sending it uses 보내다 with 을/를 (메시지를 보내다). Don't carry the English 'send him a message' double-object pattern straight over.
메시지.explanation: "message" is 메시지 (mesiji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 메시지를 보내요 ("I send a message"). Watch the particle attached to 메시지 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
메시지.shortExplanation: 메시지 means "message" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 메시지가 보내요 for 'I send a message'. 보내다 is transitive: 메시지를 보내요.
Marking the recipient with the object marker, e.g. 친구를 메시지를 보내요. The person who receives it takes 한테/에게: 친구한테 메시지를 보내요.
Treating 메시지 and 문자 as identical. 문자 specifically means an SMS text; for that, '문자 보낼게' is the natural phrase, while 메시지 is the broader word for any app message.

examples.en: Please send me a message.
examples.note: -아/어 주세요 = polite request

examples.en: I sent a message to my friend.
examples.note: recipient 한테 = to (a person)

examples.en: A message just came.
examples.note: 방금 = just now; subject 이 + 오다

ex.en: Oh, they have already arrived.
ex.note: 벌써 pairs well with surprise or realization.

벌써.nuance: 벌써 means 'already', but its core flavor is SURPRISE that something happened sooner than you expected — 'wow, already?'. Compare its near-twin 이미: 이미 is the neutral 'already / by now' that simply reports a completed fact (이미 끝났어요 'it's already finished', stating it), whereas 벌써 adds the emotional jolt (벌써 끝났어요? 'it's done already?!'). So a flat report prefers 이미; an astonished reaction prefers 벌써. It naturally rides with past tense and with 다('all'), and often co-occurs with the exclamatory endings -네요/-군요. Register-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall: don't pair 벌써 with the future — English 'already' can sit oddly with plans, but 벌써 is about something that has ALREADY occurred, so it takes past/completed verbs (벌써 갔어요), not 벌써 갈 거예요. Use 곧/이미 곧 logic for 'soon' instead.
벌써.explanation: "already" is 벌써 (beolsseo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 벌써 왔어요 ("you're here already?!"). Watch the particle attached to 벌써 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
벌써.shortExplanation: 벌써 means "already" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Attaching 벌써 to future actions: 벌써 갈 거예요 is wrong. 벌써 needs a completed event — 벌써 갔어요 ('already left').
Swapping in 벌써 where you only want a neutral report. To plainly state a fact, 이미 is better; 벌써 injects surprise you may not intend.
Word order: 끝났어요 벌써 follows English; Korean puts it first — 벌써 끝났어요.

examples.en: Is it lunchtime already?
examples.note: Simple: 벌써 voices surprise that time passed fast.

examples.en: I've already finished that book.
examples.note: Everyday: with past tense + 다, 벌써 stresses 'done sooner than expected'.

examples.en: The snow has already melted. It must be spring.
examples.note: Real situation: 벌써 + the surprise-marker -네요 conveys mild astonishment.

cluster.title: 벌써 vs 이미 vs 아직
cluster.rule: 벌써 and 이미 differ in tone, not timing: 벌써 reacts with surprise ("already?!"), while 이미 just reports a settled fact. 아직 is the opposite pole — "not yet" with a negative verb, "still" with a positive one.

members.hint: "already?!" with the surprise built in

members.en: already (it's done and can't be changed)
members.hint: the neutral "already", no reaction
"not yet" with 안, "still" without

ex.ko: 서류를 미리 준비했더라면 접수를 놓치지 않았을 텐데요.
ex.en: If I had prepared the documents in advance, I would not have missed the application.
ex.note: 준비했더라면 turns a practical mistake into a counterfactual condition.

준비하다.nuance: 준비하다 comes from 한자 準備 (準 'standard, level' + 備 'provide, equip'), literally 'get equipped to standard' — to ready things or yourself beforehand. It naturally collocates with events and outcomes: 시험을 준비하다, 여행을 준비하다, 저녁을 준비하다, 마음의 준비. Compare 마련하다 ('arrange/procure' funds or a place — 집을 마련하다) and 챙기다 ('gather up, pack' your own belongings — 여권 챙겼어? = did you grab your passport?); 준비하다 is the broad 'prepare,' while 챙기다 zooms in on not forgetting items. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'prepare FOR the exam' tempts 시험에 준비하다, but Korean treats the exam as a direct object — 시험을 준비하다. Also don't reach for 만들다 'make' when you only mean getting ready. As a 하다 verb, negate inside (준비 안 해요), and its passive 준비되다 ('be ready') is everywhere: 준비됐어요.
준비하다.explanation: 준비하다 (junbihada) = "to prepare". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 준비해요 plus one useful sentence like 저녁을 준비해요. ("I prepare dinner."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 준비하고 싶어요 for what you want, 준비할 수 있어요 for what you can, 준비 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
준비하다.shortExplanation: 준비하다 means "to prepare" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 준비하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 준비해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Wrong particle: '시험에 준비해요' for 'prepare for the exam.' Korean uses the object marker: 시험을 준비해요.
Using 만들다 (make) for getting ready: 'dinner is being prepared' is 저녁을 준비해요, not 저녁을 만들어요 unless you stress the cooking itself.
Saying '준비해요' to answer 'Are you ready?' The state 'I'm ready' is the passive 준비됐어요 / 준비됐어; 준비해요 means the act of preparing.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 준비하다 becomes 준비할 수 있어요 ("can") and 준비할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Meal + 을/를 + 준비하다; getting food ready.

examples.en: Did you get the food ready?
examples.note: Casual; 밥 stands in for 'a meal' generally.

examples.en: I have to prepare for tomorrow's presentation.
examples.note: 준비해야 하다 expresses the obligation to get ready.

examples.en: Prepare the gift in advance (and keep it ready).
examples.note: 준비해 두다 = prepare and leave set; 미리 reinforces 'ahead of time.'

ex.ko: 지훈이가 예매 시간 다시 확인해 보래요.
ex.en: Jihoon says to double-check the booking time.
ex.note: -아/어 보라고 해요 contracts to -아/어 보래요.

확인하다.nuance: 확인하다 (確認하다, 確 'certain/firm' + 認 'recognize') means to check, verify, or confirm that something is correct or true — facts, times, reservations, messages — making sure reality matches what you expect. The crucial contrast is with 찾다, which English 'check' can blur: 찾다 is 'to look FOR / search' something not yet located (열쇠를 찾다, 'look for the keys'), whereas 확인하다 is 'to verify' something you can already see (열쇠가 있는지 확인하다, 'check whether the keys are there'). It also differs from 알아보다 ('look into/inquire to find out', 가격을 알아보다). It's a regular noun+하다 verb: 확인하 + 여요 → 확인해요, past 확인했어요, with 안/못 splitting before 하다 (확인 안 해요, 확인 못 해요). English-speaker pitfall: 'check the box' or 'check off' is NOT 확인하다 — ticking a box is 체크하다/표시하다; and 'check out a book/check out (a hotel)' uses 빌리다 or 체크아웃하다, not 확인하다, which strictly means 'verify/confirm'.
확인하다.explanation: "to check" in Korean is 확인하다 (hwaginhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 확인해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 확인하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 이메일을 확인하다 ("to check email") — then reshape the same stem into 확인하고 싶어요 (desire), 확인할 수 있어요 (ability), and 확인 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
확인하다.shortExplanation: 확인하다 means "to check" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 확인하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 확인해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 확인하다 for 'look for/search' — finding something lost is 찾다 (지갑을 찾다); 확인하다 verifies something you can already check.
Saying 확인하다 for 'check (tick) a box' — that's 체크하다/표시하다; 확인하다 means confirm/verify, not mark.
Splitting as 못 확인해요 — the standard negative for a noun+하다 verb is 확인 못 해요 / 확인 안 해요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 확인하다 becomes 확인할 수 있어요 ("can") and 확인할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: 확인하다 = verify/confirm the content; 이메일을 확인해요

examples.en: I check my email.
examples.note: Noun+하다 compound, regular: stem 확인하 + 여요 → 확인해요

examples.en: I have to check the time before leaving.
examples.note: -기 전에 ('before doing'); 확인해야 해요 expresses obligation

examples.en: Please check whether this address is correct.
examples.note: -는지 embeds the yes/no question; 확인해 주세요 requests the favor

챙기다.en: to take along, to look after

ex.en: My senior says to be sure to bring your ID.
ex.note: Reminders from a senior almost always arrive as -래요.

챙기다.nuance: 챙기다 is one of the most useful 'caring' verbs in daily Korean, with a cluster of related senses: (1) gather/pack the things you need (짐을 챙기다), (2) make sure not to skip something, especially food (밥 챙겨 먹어 'make sure you eat'), and (3) look after a person attentively (동생 좀 챙겨 'keep an eye on your sibling'). Set it against 돌보다 (care for over time, like nursing a child or the sick): 챙기다 is quicker, more about 'making sure / not letting slip', while 돌보다 is sustained nurturing. It also contrasts with 챙겨 주다, where adding 주다 makes the care explicitly a favour for someone. The English trap is reaching for 들다 'lift' or 가지다 'have' when you mean 'grab/remember to bring' — that everyday act is 챙기다. Native warmth: 잘 챙겨 먹어요 is a standard way to say 'take care of yourself'.
챙기다.explanation: 챙기다 (chaenggida) means "to take care of". Start from the polite form 챙겨요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 챙기다. A strong first sentence is 짐을 챙기다 ("to pack/gather one's things"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 챙기다 also becomes 챙기고 싶어요 (want), 챙길 수 있어요 (can), and 못 챙겨요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
챙기다.shortExplanation: 챙기다 means "to take care of" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 챙기다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 챙겨요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 들다 'to lift' for 'remember to bring an umbrella' — 우산을 들어요 means physically holding it up; 'grab/take it along' is 우산을 챙겨요.
Saying 밥을 먹어 to tell someone to take care of themselves, missing the nuance — Koreans say 밥 잘 챙겨 먹어 ('make sure you eat'), where 챙기다 carries the care.
Treating 챙기다 as only 'pack objects' and never using it for people; 아이를 챙기다 / 동생을 챙기다 ('look after') is just as common.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 챙기다 becomes 챙길 수 있어요 ("can") and 챙길 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not take care of.
I want to take care of.
I have to take care of.

usagePhrases.note: Grabbing the items you need before leaving

examples.en: Grab an umbrella!
examples.note: Bare casual reminder; object 우산 with no particle

examples.ko: 나갈 때 지갑이랑 열쇠를 꼭 챙기세요.
examples.romanization: nagal ttae jigabirang yeolsoereul kkok chaenggiseyo.
examples.en: Be sure to take your wallet and keys when you leave.
examples.note: 꼭 'without fail' + 챙기다 = don't forget to grab

examples.ko: 엄마가 매일 제 도시락을 챙겨 주시고 건강도 챙겨 주세요.
examples.romanization: eommaga maeil je dosirageul chaenggyeo jusigo geongangdo chaenggyeo juseyo.
examples.en: Mom packs my lunch every day and looks after my health too.
examples.note: Shows both senses: pack things AND care for a person

ex.en: This door only opens if you tap your employee card.
ex.note: Never say 열려지다 — that stacks two passives.

열리다.nuance: 열다 needs an actor opening something. 열리다 lets the opened thing become the subject.
열리다.explanation: 열리다 (yeollida) = "to open; to be opened". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 문이 열려 있어요. ("The door is open.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 열리다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
열리다.shortExplanation: 열리다 means "to open; to be opened" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 문을 열려 있어요. The thing in the state takes 이/가: 문이 열려 있어요.
Use 열고 있어요 only when someone is actively opening it right now.

usagePhrases.note: The window became open and remains that way.

examples.en: The cafe door is still open.
examples.note: 아직 plus result-state is very natural.

켜지다.en: to come on, to be turned on

ex.ko: 센서가 있어서 사람이 지나가면 불이 켜져요.
ex.en: There's a sensor, so the light comes on when someone walks past.
ex.note: 켜다 has no -이/히/리/기- passive, so it uses -어지다.

켜지다.nuance: 켜다 is the action of turning something on. 켜지다 focuses on the thing becoming or being on.
켜지다.explanation: 켜지다 (kyeojida) means "to turn on; to be turned on". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 불이 켜져 있어요. ("The light is on."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 켜지다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
켜지다.shortExplanation: 켜지다 means "to turn on; to be turned on" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 불을 켜져 있어요. Say 불이 켜져 있어요.
Use 켜고 있어요 only when someone is in the act of turning it on.

examples.ko: 방에 불이 켜져 있어서 누가 있는 줄 알았어요.
examples.romanization: bange buri kyeojyeo isseoseo nuga inneun jul arasseoyo.
examples.en: The light was on in the room, so I thought someone was there.
examples.note: Result-state gives the visual clue.

막히다.en: to get blocked, to be jammed

ex.en: It's the weekend, so the highway is really jammed.
ex.note: 길이 막히다 is the everyday way to talk about traffic.

막히다.nuance: 막히다 is the passive/intransitive partner of the transitive 막다 ('to block'): the -히- infix turns 'someone blocks X' into 'X gets blocked', so 막히다 is something that HAPPENS to a road, drain, or nose rather than something you do. For traffic this is the single most useful verb — 길이 막히다 / 차가 막히다 — and its opposite is 뚫리다 ('to open up/clear'), with 안 막히다 the everyday 'no traffic'. Do not confuse it with 막다 itself: 'I block the road' is 길을 막다, but 'the road is jammed' is 길이 막히다, and the particle flips from 을 to 이/가 accordingly. Register is plain and universal. Because the subject is a non-person, the polite/imperative-looking forms (막혀 주세요, 막힐까요?) are essentially never used about traffic. The big English-speaker trap is treating it as transitive: there is no 'I am blocked by traffic' with you as subject — Korean puts the ROAD in the subject slot (길이 막혀요), and you simply say 길이 막혀서 늦었어요 ('I was late because the road was jammed').
막히다.explanation: 막히다 (makhi-da) = "to be blocked". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 막혀요 plus one useful sentence like 길이 막히다 ("for the road to be congested"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 막히고 싶어요 for what you want, 막힐 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 막혀요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off.
막히다.shortExplanation: 막히다 means "to be blocked" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 막히다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 막혀요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 저는 막혀요 to mean 'I'm stuck in traffic'. 막히다 takes the ROAD as subject, not the person: 길이 막혀요, then 그래서 늦었어요.
Mixing up 막다 and 막히다. 길을 막다 = 'to block the road (actively)'; 길이 막히다 = 'the road is congested'. Watch the particle: 을 for the active verb, 이/가 for the passive one.
Using 막히다 for a person standing in your way. A person blocking you is 길을 막다 (they actively block) or 앞을 가로막다; 막히다 is reserved for roads, pipes, and noses.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 막히다 becomes 막힐 수 있어요 ("can") and 막힐 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: for the road to be congested
usagePhrases.note: 길 + 이 막히다 is THE everyday way to say 'traffic is bad'

examples.en: The road is congested.
examples.note: Core frame: 길 takes subject 이, the verb is intransitive

examples.en: The road was very jammed because it was rush hour.
examples.note: Everyday: 퇴근 시간이라 'because it's leaving-work time' gives the cause

examples.ko: 지금 출발하면 차가 막혀서 두 시간 걸릴 거예요.
examples.romanization: jigeum chulbalhamyeon chaga makyeoseo du sigan geollil geoyeyo.
examples.en: If you leave now traffic will be bad and it'll take two hours.
examples.note: Real situation: 막혀서 chains cause to the 걸리다 'take time' result

ex.ko: 버스를 놓치지 않았더라면 늦지 않았을 텐데요.
ex.en: If I had not missed the bus, I would not have been late.
ex.note: Use 놓치다 for transport, chances, deadlines, and timing.

놓치다.nuance: 놓치다 is for missing something you were actively trying to catch or hold — a bus, a train, a flight, a chance, or even the thread of a conversation (요점을 놓치다 = 'miss the point') — and it always takes a 을/를 object. Its make-up shows the meaning: 놓다 ('to let go/release') + 치다, so it literally pictures something slipping out of your grasp. The single biggest English-speaker pitfall is using it for missing a *person*: English 'I miss you' is NOT 놓치다 — that is 보고 싶다 ('want to see'), so 엄마가 보고 싶어요, never 엄마를 놓쳐요. Contrast 놓치다 ('fail to catch what was within reach') with 지나가다/지나치다 ('let pass / pass by'): you 놓치다 a bus you ran for, but a chance that quietly 지나가다 simply went by. It is a regular ㅣ-stem verb: 놓치 + 어 → 놓쳐요, and it frequently appears alongside 늦다 ('be late').
놓치다.explanation: 놓치다 (nochida) = "to miss". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 놓쳐요 plus one useful sentence like 버스를 놓쳤어요 ("I missed the bus"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 놓치고 싶어요 for what you want, 놓칠 수 있어요 for what you can, 놓칠 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
놓치다.shortExplanation: 놓치다 means "to miss" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 놓치다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 놓쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
To say you miss a PERSON, use 보고 싶다, not 놓치다 — 놓치다 is only for missing a bus, train, chance, etc.
Don't drop the object marker: it's 버스를 놓쳤어요, since 놓치다 is transitive and needs a 을/를 object.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 놓치다 becomes 놓칠 수 있어요 ("can") and 놓칠 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: 놓치다 = fail to catch a bus/train/flight; the thing missed takes 을/를.

examples.en: I just missed the bus
examples.note: The most typical use, for transport you failed to catch.

examples.en: I was late because I missed the subway
examples.note: Pairs naturally with 늦다 in everyday excuses (-아서 gives the reason).

examples.ko: 이런 좋은 기회를 놓치면 안 돼요
examples.romanization: ireon joeun gihoereul notchimyeon an dwaeyo
examples.en: You shouldn't miss a good chance like this
examples.note: Opportunities use 놓치다 too; -면 안 되다 gives the 'mustn't' warning.

ex.en: It has been six months since I started learning Korean.
ex.note: 배우기 시작하다 marks the beginning of the learning action.

배우다.nuance: 배우다 means 'to learn / acquire a skill or subject' and takes the object marker 을/를: 한국어를 배워요. It is a regular verb, but the stem ends in the vowel 우, so when 어요 attaches the two vowels contract into 워 — 배우 + 어요 → 배워요 (not 배우어요), past 배웠어요. The natural partner verb is 가르치다 ('to teach'), the giving side of the same act; and the person you learn from takes 한테/에게서 (사람) — 선생님한테 배워요 — never the place particle 에서 for the source. Contrast 배우다 with 공부하다 (工夫하다, 'to study'): 공부하다 is the effort of studying (sitting down, reviewing, hitting the books), while 배우다 is the result of acquiring a skill or being taught it, often from someone. So you 공부하다 for an exam at your desk but 배우다 the piano from a teacher. The English-speaker pitfall is writing the uncontracted 배우어요, and saying 학원에서 배우다 to mean 'learn from the academy' — 에서 marks where, while the human source must take 한테/에게서.
배우다.explanation: 배우다 (baeuda) = "to learn". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 배워요 plus one useful sentence like 한국어를 배워요 ("I learn Korean"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 배우고 싶어요 for what you want, 배울 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 배워요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help.
배우다.shortExplanation: 배우다 means "to learn" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 배우다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 배워요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the uncontracted 배우어요 — the 우 + 어요 contracts, so the polite present is 배워요 (past 배웠어요).
Confusing 배우다 with 공부하다 — 공부하다 is the act of studying/reviewing; 배우다 is acquiring or being taught a skill. Use 시험공부를 해요 for exam prep, 피아노를 배워요 for taking lessons.
Marking the person you learn from with 에서 — a human source takes 한테/에게서: 선생님한테 배워요, not 선생님에서.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 배우다 becomes 배울 수 있어요 ("can") and 배울 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: the subject/skill learned takes the object marker 을/를

examples.en: I learn Korean.
examples.note: two vowels contract: 배우 + 어요 → 배워요

examples.en: These days I'm learning guitar from a friend.
examples.note: source person takes 한테; 고 있다 = ongoing

examples.ko: 저는 운전을 배워서 회사에 차로 가고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun unjeoneul baewoseo hoesae charo gago sipeoyo.
examples.en: I want to learn to drive and go to work by car.
examples.note: real goal-linked sentence; 배워서 connects reason to plan

ex.en: If I had solved the last question, I would have passed.
ex.note: 합격하다 belongs naturally in exam-regret counterfactuals.

합격하다.nuance: 합격하다 is Sino-Korean 合格 — 合 'meet/match' + 格 'standard' — literally 'meet the standard', i.e. clear a cut-off and pass a test, interview, or admissions screen. Its opposite is 불합격하다 (不合格) or, much more colloquially, 떨어지다 'to fall/drop' (시험에 떨어졌어요 = I failed/flunked). Don't confuse 합격하다 with 통과하다 'to pass through': 통과하다 is moving past a checkpoint or a bill passing, while 합격하다 specifically means meeting a qualifying standard. The headline English-speaker pitfall is the particle: English 'pass THE exam' (object) makes learners write 시험을 합격하다, but Korean uses 에 — 시험에 합격하다 — because you're 'matching up TO the standard'. Note also 합격하다 (verb) vs 합격 (the noun, 'a pass/acceptance'): the noun is what you put on banners — 합격 축하해! As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (합격해요, 합격했어요, formal 합격합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (합격 안 해요, 합격 못 해요).
합격하다.explanation: "to pass an exam" in Korean is 합격하다 (hapgyeokada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 합격해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 합격하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 시험에 합격하다 ("to pass the exam / make the cut") — then reshape the same stem into 합격하고 싶어요 (desire), 합격할 수 있어요 (ability), and 합격 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
합격하다.shortExplanation: 합격하다 means "to pass an exam" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 합격하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 합격해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 시험을 합격했어요 because English treats the exam as a direct object — Korean marks it with 에: 시험에 합격했어요.
Using 합격하다 to mean a course or class 'passed' in the sense of finishing it — for clearing a checkpoint generally use 통과하다; 합격하다 = meeting a qualifying standard.
Forming 'I failed' as 합격 안 했어요, which sounds oddly neutral ('didn't pass') — the natural opposite Koreans say is 떨어졌어요 (시험에 떨어졌어요).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 합격하다 becomes 합격할 수 있어요 ("can") and 합격할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not pass an exam.
I want to pass an exam.
I have to pass an exam.
to pass the exam / make the cut
usagePhrases.note: what you pass takes 에: 시험에 합격해요 (NOT 시험을)

examples.en: I passed the exam!
examples.note: Use 에 for the thing passed; the past 합격했어요 reports the result

examples.en: This time I really want to pass.
examples.note: 꼭 = for sure/without fail; 이번에는 = this time around

examples.ko: 공부를 안 하면 합격 못 해요.
examples.romanization: gongbureul an hamyeon hapgyeong mo taeyo.
examples.en: If you don't study, you can't pass.
examples.note: ~면 = if; impossible form splits: 합격 못 해요

ex.ko: 조금만 일찍 도착했더라면 시험을 볼 수 있었을 거예요.
ex.en: If I had arrived just a little earlier, I could have taken the exam.
ex.note: 시험을 보다 is the fixed phrase for taking an exam.

시험.nuance: 시험 is Sino-Korean 試驗 — 試 'try/test' + 驗 'examine', literally 'a trial examination'. The collocation English speakers must memorize is 시험을 보다 — Koreans 'see' an exam, they do not 'do' it, so 시험을 하다 is wrong. Passing and failing are vivid metaphors with the particle 에: 시험에 붙다 (literally 'stick to the exam') = pass, 시험에 떨어지다 ('fall off the exam') = fail — note these take 에, not 을. Contrast 시험 with 퀴즈(quiz, a small in-class test) and with 검사(檢査, an inspection/medical test like 건강 검사): a graded school test is always 시험, never 퀴즈 unless it is a tiny informal one. The classic 직역 trap is 'take an exam' → 시험을 가지다/취하다 ✗ (English 'take' never transfers); and learners often write 시험을 통과하다, which is understandable but bookish — the everyday word is 붙다.
시험.explanation: 시험 (siheom) = "exam". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 시험을 보다 ("take an exam") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 시험, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.
시험.shortExplanation: 시험 means "exam" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 시험을 하다 instead of 시험을 보다. Koreans 'see/look at' an exam (보다); 하다 does not collocate with 시험.
Using 를 for pass/fail: 시험을 붙다 ✗. The verbs 붙다/떨어지다 take 에 — 시험에 붙다/떨어지다.
Translating 'take the exam' as 시험을 가지다 ('have/hold'). English 'take' is not literal here; the only natural verb is 보다.

usagePhrases.note: Fixed verb is 보다 (literally 'see'), never 하다
Existence/scheduling; the exam is the subject, so 이
붙다 'stick' = pass, 떨어지다 'fall' = fail; both take 에
기말(期末) = end of term; cf. 중간 시험 = midterm

examples.en: Is there an exam tomorrow?
examples.note: Casual; 있어요 used for a scheduled event existing

examples.en: I took the Korean exam yesterday.
examples.note: 봤어요 = past of 보다; the set phrase 시험을 보다

examples.en: I studied hard so I passed the exam.
examples.note: Pass = 시험에 붙다; note the particle is 에, not 를

ex.en: For my health, I decided to walk every day.
ex.note: Noun + 을 위해 is the noun version of V-기 위해.

건강.nuance: 건강 is Sino-Korean 健康, where 健 means 'sturdy/robust' and 康 means 'peaceful/well,' together the sound, robust state of body and mind. It splits into a noun and an adjective: the noun 건강 ('health') pairs with 좋다/나쁘다 (good/bad) — never 높다/낮다 (high/low), which is the typical English-influenced slip from 'high level of health' — and you actively mind it with 챙기다 (건강을 챙기다, 'look after your health'); the adjective 건강하다 means 'to be healthy' (저는 건강해요 = 'I'm healthy'). Its honorific imperative 건강하세요 is a beloved set phrase, a warm farewell/blessing meaning 'stay healthy,' especially said to elders and at New Year. A near-synonym is 컨디션 (a loanword from 'condition') — but 컨디션 is your day-to-day fitness/energy level (오늘 컨디션이 안 좋아 = 'I'm not feeling great today'), whereas 건강 is your overall, long-term state of wellness; don't swap them.
건강.explanation: 건강 (geongang) = "health". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 건강이 좋아요 ("my health is good") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 건강, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.
건강.shortExplanation: 건강 means "health" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 건강이 높아요 for good health: health is 좋다/나쁘다, so it must be 건강이 좋아요.
Confusing 건강 with 컨디션: long-term wellness is 건강; today's energy/feeling is 컨디션.
Saying 건강이세요 instead of 건강하세요: the blessing comes from the adjective 건강하다, giving 건강하세요.

usagePhrases.note: 좋다, not 높다, describes good health
챙기다 = take care of, mind one's health

examples.en: Health is the most important thing.
examples.note: Simple: 건강이 + adjective, the core 'health is X' frame.

examples.ko: 요즘 운동을 시작해서 건강이 많이 좋아졌어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum undongeul sijakaeseo geongangi mani joajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I started exercising lately, so my health has improved a lot.
examples.note: Everyday: 운동을 시작하다 + 건강이 좋아지다 (improve).

examples.en: Grandma, please always stay healthy and live a long, long life.
examples.note: Real-situation: honorific 건강하시다 + 사세요 as a warm blessing.

ex.en: I am building a habit of listening every day.
ex.note: -는 습관 naturally describes repeated behavior.

습관.nuance: 습관 (習慣, 習 'to practice/learn' + 慣 'to grow accustomed') frames a habit as something drilled in until it feels natural, and it leans slightly formal and neutral. The key contrast is 습관 vs 버릇: 습관 is a broad, often deliberate routine (early rising, daily exercise, good study habits), while 버릇 is colloquial and usually a quirky or annoying unconscious tic — nail-biting, leg-shaking, a child's bad manners. Crucially, scolding a child you say 버릇없다 ('has no manners / is rude'), never 습관없다. Both pair with 고치다 ('fix') for breaking them and 들이다/생기다 for forming them (습관을 들이다 = cultivate a habit; 습관이 생기다 = a habit forms). To say you have one, use 습관이 있다. Pitfall: English 'I have a habit of doing X' must use the verb's -는 present-modifier form before 습관: 일찍 자는 습관 (the habit of sleeping early), not 일찍 자기 습관. Also do not use 가지다 here — habits 있다/되다/생기다, they are not 'had' with 가지다.
습관.explanation: 습관 (seupgwan) means "habit". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이것은 좋은 습관이에요. ("This is a good habit."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 습관 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
습관.shortExplanation: 습관 means "habit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Forming 'have a habit of ~ing' wrongly: 운동하기 습관 is broken. Use the -는 modifier: 운동하는 습관이 있어요.
Using 습관 for a child's rudeness. 'That kid is rude/ill-mannered' is 그 아이는 버릇이 없어요, not 습관이 없어요.
Saying 습관을 가지고 있어요 by translating 'have a habit'. The idiomatic verb is 있다 or 되다: 습관이 있어요 / 습관이 됐어요.

usagePhrases.note: 좋은/나쁜 + 습관 describes the quality of a habit

usagePhrases.en: I want to fix a bad habit.
usagePhrases.note: 습관을 고치다 = 'correct/break a habit'; 고치다 = repair
습관이 되다 = 'turn into a habit', now automatic

usagePhrases.en: I have a habit of going to bed early.
usagePhrases.note: verb + -는 + 습관이 있다 = 'have the habit of ~ing'

examples.en: I have a habit of exercising every morning.
examples.note: -는 습관이 있다 is the frame for stating any routine

examples.en: I changed my coffee-drinking habit.
examples.note: 습관을 바꾸다 = 'change a habit' (swap it), milder than 고치다

examples.en: I can't break my nail-biting habit.
examples.note: Here a small bad tic is a 버릇, not 습관 — note the register difference

ex.en: The meeting room was suddenly changed to the third floor.
