ex.note: 바꾸다 plus -이- gives 바뀌다; nobody has to be blamed for the change.

바뀌다.nuance: 바뀌다 is the intransitive twin of 바꾸다: the thing that changes is itself the subject (이/가) and nobody is named as the doer, so it covers things getting switched, replaced, or mixed up on their own. The dividing line vs 변하다 is key — 변하다 means a thing's inner nature transforms (사람이 변했다 = he's become a different person), while 바뀌다 means one item is swapped out for another (번호가 바뀌었다 = the number was replaced). Use 바꾸다 when YOU actively swap something (번호를 바꿨어요) and 바뀌다 when it simply ends up different (번호가 바뀌었어요). The 요-form is 바뀌어요 because the stem ends in the vowel 위, which won't contract — so spelling matters: it's 바뀌-, and the polite past is 바뀌었어요, never the wrong 바껴요/바꼈어요 that English speakers reach for by analogy.
바뀌다.explanation: "to change, to be switched" in Korean is 바뀌다 (bakkwida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 바뀌어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 바뀌다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 비밀번호가 바뀌었어요. ("The password changed.") — then reshape the same stem into 바뀌고 싶어요 (desire), 바뀔 수 있어요 (ability), and 바뀔 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
바뀌다.shortExplanation: 바뀌다 means "to change, to be switched" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 바뀌다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 바뀌어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 바뀌다 transitively — '번호를 바뀌었어요' is wrong because 바뀌다 has no object. If YOU did it, use 바꾸다: 번호를 바꿨어요.
Don't write the polite form as 바껴요 or the past as 바꼈어요; the 바뀌- stem keeps its 위 and gives 바뀌어요 / 바뀌었어요.
Don't blur 바뀌다 and 변하다: 마음이 바뀌었어요 = I changed my mind (switched decisions), but 마음이 변했어요 = my feelings have transformed (e.g., fallen out of love).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 바뀌다 becomes 바뀔 수 있어요 ("can") and 바뀔 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not change, to be switched.
I want to change, to be switched.
I can change, to be switched.
I have to change, to be switched.

usagePhrases.note: 바뀌다 = something gets switched/replaced by something else. The thing that changes takes 이/가, never 을/를.

examples.en: The meeting time got changed to 3 o'clock.
examples.note: Super common at work — schedules and times 'get changed' on you; note 3시로 with (으)로.

examples.en: Oh, the shop's name changed.
examples.note: ~네요 adds a 'huh, I just noticed' tone — natural the moment you spot a change.

examples.en: The plan might change again.
examples.note: 또 (again) + 바뀌다 is the everyday way to warn that things aren't fixed yet.

ex.ko: 그때 선택을 바꿨더라면 지금 상황이 달라졌을 거예요.
ex.en: If I had changed my choice then, the situation would be different now.
ex.note: 달라졌을 거예요 is a natural result clause for counterfactuals.

달라지다.nuance: 달라지다 spotlights the before-and-after gap: something is now clearly unlike how it used to be, which makes it the everyday verb for noticing change in a person's looks, mood, or a situation. It's the inchoative of the adjective 다르다 (to be different) — 다르 + -아지다 'become' — and that origin is the #1 pitfall: 다르다 states a static difference between two things (A는 B와 달라요 = A is different from B), while 달라지다 is the dynamic act of becoming different over time (분위기가 달라졌어요 = the mood changed). It overlaps with 변하다 and 바뀌다, but the dividing line is focus: 달라지다 = 'the result looks different now,' 변하다 = 'the inner nature transformed,' 바뀌다 = 'one thing got swapped for another.' Both 달라지다 and the thing changing take 이/가; the form 달라져요 comes from -지다 verbs taking 어 in the 요-form (지+어 → 져).
달라지다.explanation: 달라지다 (dallajida) = "to become different, to change". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 달라져요 plus one useful sentence like 분위기가 완전히 달라졌어요. ("The atmosphere became completely different."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 달라지고 싶어요 for what you want, 달라질 수 있어요 for what you can, 달라질 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
달라지다.shortExplanation: 달라지다 means "to become different, to change" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 달라지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 달라져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't confuse it with 다르다 — 다르다 is an adjective for a static difference (저는 형과 성격이 달라요), while 달라지다 is a verb for becoming different (성격이 달라졌어요).
It's intransitive, so don't attach 을/를: say 생각이 달라졌어요, not 생각을 달라졌어요. To deliberately change something, use 바꾸다.
Don't say the present as 달라요 when you mean 'is changing'; 달라요 = 'is different (now)', 달라지고 있어요 = 'is becoming different'.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 달라지다 becomes 달라질 수 있어요 ("can") and 달라질 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not become different, to change.
I want to become different, to change.
I can become different, to change.
I have to become different, to change.

usagePhrases.note: 달라지다 = end up noticeably different from before. Built from 다르다 (be different) + -아지다.

examples.en: Did you cut your hair? You look different.
examples.note: Great compliment-ish line — 느낌이 달라지다 = the vibe/impression changed.

examples.en: Now that I've lived here, my thinking has changed a lot.
examples.note: Use for gradual inner change — 생각이/가치관이 달라지다.

examples.en: The rules will be different starting next year.
examples.note: Common in notices about policies, fees, or schedules changing.

ex.ko: 조금만 일찍 나왔으면 버스를 놓치지 않았을 텐데요.
ex.en: If I had left just a little earlier, I would not have missed the bus.
ex.note: 조금만 일찍 is a very natural regret chunk.

일찍.nuance: 일찍 means 'early' in the sense of an EARLY POINT IN TIME — early hour of the day or ahead of a schedule — and is the natural opposite of 늦게(late). The classic confusion is 일찍 vs 빨리: 일찍 is about WHEN on the clock (일찍 일어나요 = 'wake up at an early hour'), while 빨리 is about SPEED/quickness (빨리 일어나요 = 'get up quick!'). So '일찍 오세요' invites someone to arrive at an early time, whereas '빨리 오세요' urges them to hurry. It pairs habitually with 자다, 일어나다, 출근하다, 도착하다, 출발하다. Register-neutral and polite-safe. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 일찍/빨리 mix-up, since English 'early' and 'fast/quick' feel adjacent but map to two different Korean adverbs; also remember 일찍 is an adverb already, so you never conjugate it like the adjective 이르다.
일찍.explanation: "early" is 일찍 (iljjik). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 일찍 자요 ("I sleep early"). Watch the particle attached to 일찍 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
일찍.shortExplanation: 일찍 means "early" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 빨리 when you mean 'at an early hour'. 빨리 자요 means 'sleep quickly'; to say 'sleep early (in the evening)' use 일찍 자요.
Trying to conjugate it as if it were an adjective. 일찍 is the fixed adverb; you don't say 일찍어요. The related adjective is 이르다 ('to be early').
Word order: 와요 일찍 mirrors English; Korean puts the adverb first — 일찍 와요.

examples.en: I usually sleep early.
examples.note: Simple: 일찍 = at an early hour, before 자요.

examples.en: Tomorrow I want to get up early.
examples.note: Everyday: 일찍 + 일어나다 is the standard 'wake up early' collocation.

examples.en: Worried about traffic, I left thirty minutes early.
examples.note: Real situation: 일찍 here means 'ahead of schedule', and 30분 일찍 = 'earlier by 30 min'.

cluster.title: 빨리 vs 일찍 vs 어서
cluster.rule: 빨리 is about speed and 일찍 is about the clock: 빨리 오세요 means 'get here quick', 일찍 오세요 means 'come at an early hour'. 어서 also pushes for speed but sounds warm and welcoming, so it lives in polite invitations like 어서 오세요.

members.hint: about speed, and can sound impatient
about the clock, not the speed
warm urging, mostly with polite invitations

ex.ko: 동생은 눈을 감고 자는 척하고 있었어요.
ex.en: My sibling had their eyes shut, pretending to be asleep.
ex.note: A verb in progress, so it takes -는 척하다 rather than -(으)ㄴ.

자다.nuance: 자다 becomes 잘 before some future or ability forms: 잘 거예요, 잘 수 있어요.
자다.explanation: "to sleep" in Korean is 자다 (jada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 자요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 자다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 잘 자요 ("sleep well / good night.") — then reshape the same stem into 자고 싶어요 (desire), 잘 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 자요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
자다.shortExplanation: 자다 means "to sleep" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 자다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 자요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
자 주세요 is grammatically possible, but 잘 자요 is the natural phrase for “good night.” Use request forms only with a real context.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 자다 becomes 잘 수 있어요 ("can") and 잘 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

examples.en: I sleep early today.
examples.note: Daily routine.

examples.en: I could not sleep well yesterday.
examples.note: Common complaint.

examples.en: Shall we sleep now?
examples.note: Suggestion.

ex.en: It is not as hard as I thought.
ex.note: This word naturally triggers realization endings because expectation changed.

생각보다.nuance: 생각보다 naturally pairs with 더라고요 because both talk about what you found after experience.
생각보다.explanation: 생각보다 (saenggakboda) = "more/less than expected". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 생각보다 괜찮다 ("to be better than expected") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 생각보다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
생각보다.shortExplanation: 생각보다 means "more/less than expected" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 생각보다 without saying what was different from expectation.
Confusing 생각보다 with 그냥 생각. 생각보다 is a comparison phrase.

usagePhrases.note: Often used with 나오다 or 끝나다.

examples.en: The food came out faster than expected, I noticed.
examples.note: Expectation plus firsthand observation.

붐비다.en: to be crowded, to be packed

ex.ko: 지하철이 너무 붐비는 바람에 한 대를 그냥 보냈어요.
ex.en: The subway was so packed that I just let one train go.
ex.note: A crowd is not your doing, so -는 바람에 is the natural connector.

붐비다.nuance: 붐비다 describes the place or route becoming crowded. 사람이 많다 describes the number of people more directly.
붐비다.explanation: 붐비다 (bumbida) = "to be crowded". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 식당이 붐비다 ("the restaurant is crowded") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 붐비다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
붐비다.shortExplanation: 붐비다 means "to be crowded" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 붐비다 for one person being busy. For a busy person, use 바쁘다.
Forgetting that 붐비다 usually needs a place or traffic-like subject.

examples.en: It was quiet at first, and then it quickly got crowded, I noticed.
examples.note: A natural restaurant or event observation.

ex.en: A customer is asking whether there's parking. Shall I go ask?
ex.note: -냬요 already means "is asking", so you rarely need 물어보다 twice in one sentence.

물어보다.nuance: 묻다 is the dictionary/base verb. 물어보다 is often the natural spoken choice for asking someone.
물어보다.explanation: 물어보다 (mureoboda) = "to ask; to ask and find out". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 친구한테 물어보다 ("to ask a friend") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 물어보다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
물어보다.shortExplanation: 물어보다 means "to ask; to ask and find out" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 묻다 forms mechanically when 물어보다 sounds more natural in conversation.
Forgetting the person marker: 친구한테 물어봤어요 or 선생님께 물어봤어요.

usagePhrases.en: to ask what time it is

examples.en: My friend asked what time we are meeting.
examples.note: Reported question with the everyday verb 물어보다.

cluster.title: 묻다 vs 물어보다 vs 질문하다
cluster.rule: 물어보다 is what people actually say out loud; 묻다 is the same act but terser and more written (and ㄷ-irregular, so it becomes 물어요). 질문하다 is "ask a question" where questions are a formal event — a class, a meeting, a Q&A.

members.hint: the bookish "ask" — ㄷ-irregular, 물어요

example.en: I asked for directions at the station.

members.en: to ask; to ask and find out
members.hint: the normal spoken "ask" — use this one
asking a question in a formal setting

example.en: I asked a question during class.

전하다.en: to pass on, to convey (a message)

ex.ko: 팀장님이 회의 시간이 바뀌었다고 팀원들한테 전하래요.
ex.en: The team lead says to tell the team members that the meeting time has changed.
ex.note: 전하다 is the verb for being the messenger, which is exactly what these endings do.

전하다.nuance: 전하다 (Sino-Korean 傳, 'transmit/hand down') means relaying something from a sender to a receiver: a message, regards, an item, news, or even a feeling, so the receiver takes 에게/한테 or honorific 께 while the thing passed takes 을/를. The nearest rival is 말하다, but 말하다 is you simply saying something yourself, whereas 전하다 stresses that you are the go-between carrying someone else's words or goods to a third party — '사장님이 잘했다고 전하래요' (the boss told me to tell you 'well done'). Everyday set phrases include 안부를 전하다 (send one's regards), 말씀 전해 주세요 (please pass on the message), and 소식을 전하다 (deliver news). The big English-speaker trap is hearing 전 and thinking 전화하다 ('to make a phone call'): they share the 전 syllable but are unrelated, so '전해 주세요' is 'please relay it', not 'please call them'.
전하다.explanation: "to convey / pass on (a message)" in Korean is 전하다 (jeonha-da). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 전해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 전하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 말 좀 전해 주세요. ("Please pass on a message for me.") — then reshape the same stem into 전하고 싶어요 (desire), 전할 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 전해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
전하다.shortExplanation: 전하다 means "to convey / pass on (a message)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 전하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 전해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Do not confuse 전하다 (pass on / convey a message) with 전화하다 (make a phone call); '말 전해 주세요' means 'relay my words', not 'phone them'.
The receiver of the message takes 에게/한테/께, not 을/를: '친구에게 전해 주세요', and the message itself is what takes 을/를.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 전하다 becomes 전할 수 있어요 ("can") and 전할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not convey / pass on (a message).
I want to convey / pass on (a message).
I can convey / pass on (a message).
I have to convey / pass on (a message).
Please pass on a message for me.
usagePhrases.note: Set phrase for relaying spoken words to someone

examples.ko: 부장님께 이 서류 좀 전해 주세요.
examples.romanization: bujangnimkke i seoryu jom jeonhae juseyo.
examples.en: Please hand this document to the manager for me.
examples.note: Note honorific 께 because the receiver is senior

examples.en: Tell my friend I said hi.
examples.note: Casual 한테 + 줘; passing on regards between friends

examples.ko: 제 마음을 어떻게 전해야 할지 모르겠어요.
examples.romanization: je maeumeul eotteoke jeonhaeya halji moreugesseoyo.
examples.en: I do not know how to convey how I feel.
examples.note: 전하다 also carries abstract things like feelings

읽히다.en: to make someone read / to be read

ex.en: The teacher had the students read the passage.
ex.note: Causative use; linked to word-ext-ch38-ilkida-passive.

읽히다.nuance: With texts, 읽히다 often describes how easily something is read or understood.
읽히다.explanation: "to be read / to make someone read" is 읽히다 (ilkida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 문장이 잘 읽히다 ("a sentence reads clearly"). Watch the particle attached to 읽히다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
읽히다.shortExplanation: 읽히다 means "to be read / to make someone read" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not pair 읽히다 with a plain active example like 책을 읽어요 when teaching this chapter.

examples.ko: 저는 그 문장이 처음에 잘 안 읽혔어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun geu munjangi cheoeume jal an ilkyeosseoyo.
examples.en: At first, that sentence did not read clearly to me.
examples.note: The text is the focus.

팔리다.en: to be sold, to sell out

ex.ko: 인기 메뉴라서 점심 전에 다 팔려요.
ex.en: It's a popular item, so it sells out before lunch.
ex.note: The goods are the subject; the seller is not mentioned.

팔리다.nuance: Use 팔리다 when the seller is not important or not known.
팔리다.explanation: 팔리다 (pallida) = "to be sold". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 다 팔리다 ("to be sold out") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 팔리다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.
팔리다.shortExplanation: 팔리다 means "to be sold" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 팔다 when the product itself should be the subject.

examples.ko: 인기 상품이 하루 만에 다 팔렸어요.
examples.romanization: ingi sangpumi haru mane da pallyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The popular product sold out in one day.
examples.note: The product is the subject.

ex.en: The pickpocket was caught by the police at the subway station.
ex.note: A human agent, so 한테 in speech and 에게 in writing.

잡히다.nuance: 잡히다 is natural for appointments, schedules, reservations, and plans.
잡히다.explanation: 잡히다 (japida) means "to be set / to be scheduled". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 일정이 잡히다 ("a schedule gets set"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 잡히다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
잡히다.shortExplanation: 잡히다 means "to be set / to be scheduled" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not translate it literally as “be grabbed” in schedule contexts.

examples.en: The meeting schedule was set for next week.
examples.note: The sentence focuses on the schedule result.

ex.ko: 지하철 문이 눈앞에서 닫혀서 한 대를 놓쳤어요.
ex.en: The subway door shut right in front of me, so I missed a train.
ex.note: Pronounced [다치다]: ㄷ plus ㅎ fuse and then palatalize.

닫히다.nuance: Use 닫히다 when you care about the closed state/result more than the person closing it.
닫히다.explanation: "to be closed" is 닫히다 (datida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 문이 닫히다 ("the door closes / is closed"). Watch the particle attached to 닫히다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
닫히다.shortExplanation: 닫히다 means "to be closed" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
닫다 needs an actor; 닫히다 lets the object become the subject.

examples.en: The door closed automatically.
examples.note: The door is the subject.

입히다.en: to dress someone / put clothing on someone

ex.en: The father put a coat on the baby.
ex.note: Linked to chapter card word-ext-ch38-iphida.

입히다.nuance: 입다 is wear; 입히다 is dress someone else.
입히다.explanation: "to dress someone / put clothing on someone" is 입히다 (ipida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 아이에게 코트를 입히다 ("to put a coat on a child"). Watch the particle attached to 입히다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
입히다.shortExplanation: 입히다 means "to dress someone / put clothing on someone" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 입다 when the subject is dressing another person.

usagePhrases.en: to put a coat on a child

examples.en: The father put a coat on the baby.
examples.note: Someone causes another person to wear clothing.

ex.en: If the explanation gets long, it will be hard to understand.
ex.note: Linked to dictionary card word-ext-1461.

설명.nuance: 설명(說明) is Sino-Korean — 說 'to tell/speak' + 明 'clear, bright' — literally 'to make clear by telling,' i.e. an explanation of how or why something works. Distinguish it from 설득(說得) 'persuasion' (talking someone INTO agreeing, sharing the 說 root) and from 묘사(描寫) 'description' (depicting what something looks/feels like); 설명 is about clarifying and informing, not convincing or portraying. As a noun it becomes the verb with 하다: 설명하다, very often softened to 설명해 주세요/주시겠어요 'please explain for me.' Collocations: 설명을 하다/듣다, 자세한 설명, 설명이 부족하다/이해가 안 되다, 설명서 'instruction manual.' The English-speaker pitfall: English 'explain to me' tempts learners to mark the listener with 를 (저를 설명하다 ✗, which would mean 'explain ME'); the listener takes 한테/에게 (저한테 설명해 주세요), and what you explain takes 을/를. Bare 설명 can't be the verb — use 설명하다. Don't confuse 설명 with the look-alike 설탕 'sugar.'
설명.explanation: "explanation" is 설명 (seolmyeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 설명을 하다 ("to explain, to give an explanation"). Watch the particle attached to 설명 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
설명.shortExplanation: 설명 means "explanation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Marking the listener with 를: 'explain to me' is 저한테 설명해 주세요, not 저를 설명하다 (that means 'explain me').
Using bare 설명 for 'to explain' — say 설명하다 / 설명을 하다.
Confusing 설명 (clarifying/informing) with 설득 (persuading someone) — convincing a person is 설득하다, not 설명하다.

usagePhrases.en: to explain, to give an explanation
usagePhrases.note: 설명 is a noun; 'to explain' = 설명하다 / 설명을 하다
-아/어 주세요 frames it as a favor; the polite way to ask for an explanation
자세한 'detailed' before the noun; 설명이 자세하다 puts it after
덧붙이다 = to append/add on; common in writing or talks

examples.en: Teacher, please explain it.
examples.note: 설명하다 + 주세요 = 'please explain (for me)'; softens the request

examples.en: Could you explain it one more time?
examples.note: -아/어 주시겠어요? is extra-polite; 한 번 더 = once more

examples.en: This part is a bit short on explanation.
examples.note: 설명이 부족하다 = the explanation is lacking; here 설명 is the subject (이/가)

ex.en: As for the two people, their opinions are different.
ex.note: 두 사람은 is the frame; 의견이 is the differing subject.

다르다.nuance: 다르다 is the antonym of 같다 and conjugates as a 르-irregular: the stem 다르 + 아요 doubles the ㄹ and drops 으 to give 달라요 (never 다라요); past is 달랐어요. The pre-noun form 다른 is one of the most-used words in Korean and covers both 'different' and 'another' (다른 색 = 'a different/another colour'). The dangerous trap for English speakers is 틀리다, which means 'to be wrong / incorrect' — even native speakers loosely say 틀리다 for 'different' in speech, but in correct Korean 답이 틀리다 = 'the answer is wrong' while 답이 다르다 = 'the answer is different'. Mixing them can imply someone is mistaken when you only meant they differ, which can sound rude. Pair 다르다 with 하고/와 for the thing compared: 작년하고 달라요 ('it's different from last year').
다르다.explanation: 다르다 (dareuda) means "to be different". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is N하고 다르다 ("to be different from N"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 다르다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
다르다.shortExplanation: 다르다 means "to be different" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 틀리다 ('to be wrong') to mean 'different' — standard Korean keeps them separate; 다르다 = different, 틀리다 = incorrect, and confusing them can sound like you're calling something a mistake.
Conjugating it as 다라요 — it's a 르-irregular, so the correct present form is 달라요 (and past 달랐어요).
Forgetting the comparison particle: say '이거하고 달라요', not '이거 달라요'.

usagePhrases.note: 하고 marks what it differs from; 와/과 in writing

usagePhrases.en: it differs from person to person

examples.en: The taste is a bit different.
examples.note: 좀 softens it; note 르-irregular 달라요, not 다라요

examples.en: I think differently.
examples.note: lit. 'my thought is different' — Korean states the trait, not the person, as subject

examples.ko: 사이즈가 사람마다 달라서 입어 보고 사세요.
examples.romanization: saijeuga sarammada dallaseo ibeo bogo saseyo.
examples.en: Sizes differ per person, so try it on before buying.
examples.note: real shopping advice; 마다 + 다르다 is idiomatic

ex.en: Before starting my studying, I clear my desk.
ex.note: 공부 is a noun; 공부를 시작하다 is different from 공부하기 시작하다 but both are useful.

공부.nuance: 공부(工夫)는 한자 그대로 '공을 들여 애씀'이라는 뜻으로, 지식이나 기술을 배우고 익히는 모든 활동을 가리키는 가장 기본적인 단어예요. 비슷한 말 '학습'은 교과서나 보고서에 어울리는 딱딱한 한자어라 일상 대화에서는 거의 안 쓰고, '연습'은 이미 배운 것을 몸에 익히려 반복하는 것이라 '머리로 새로 익히는' 공부와는 결이 달라요. 영어 study처럼 목적어를 바로 붙여 '공부 Korean'이라고 하면 안 되고, 반드시 '한국어를 공부하다'처럼 -을/를을 쓰거나 '한국어 공부를 하다'로 명사화해야 해요. 동사로 쓸 때 '공부를 하다'와 한 단어 '공부하다'가 둘 다 자연스럽고, '열심히/같이/매일'과 잘 어울려요.
공부.explanation: "study, studying" is 공부 (gongbu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 공부를 하다 ("study, do studying"). Watch the particle attached to 공부 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.
공부.shortExplanation: 공부 means "study, studying" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
'공부하다' 자체가 이미 동사라서 '공부를 공부해요'처럼 쓰면 같은 말을 두 번 한 셈이라 틀려요. '공부해요' 또는 '공부를 해요' 한쪽만 쓰세요.
영어 'study a book'을 직역해 '책을 공부' 또는 '공부 책'이라고 하면 안 돼요. 목적어에는 -을/를을 붙여 '책을 공부하다'라고 해야 합니다.
'나는 공부를 좋아요'는 틀려요. '좋다'는 형용사라 대상에 -이/가가 붙으니 '나는 공부가 좋아요' 또는 '공부를 좋아해요'로 써야 합니다.

usagePhrases.note: 보통 붙여서 '공부하다' 한 단어로도 자연스럽게 써요
앞에 과목·언어를 붙여 무엇을 공부하는지 밝혀요

examples.en: I study Korean every day.
examples.note: '매일'(every day)처럼 빈도 부사는 동사 앞에 둬요.

examples.en: These days studying for the exam is so tough.
examples.note: '시험 공부'는 명사 두 개를 붙여 'exam studying'을 만든 합성이에요.

examples.en: I studied together with my seatmate at the library.
examples.note: 장소는 '-에서', 동행은 구어체 '하고'로 붙여요.

ex.en: They say that team works late every single day.
ex.note: 야근하다 is a verb, so the present tense needs -ㄴ대요.

야근.nuance: 야근 specifically means staying at the office working late into the night — the iconic symbol of old-school Korean work culture. It is Sino-Korean 夜勤, literally 'night-duty', sharing the 勤 ('duty/labor') of 외근 and 출근. The contrast to nail: 야근 is overtime that runs LATE/at night, whereas 특근 (特勤, 'special duty') and 추가 근무 cover extra work generally, including daytime, weekends, or holidays — so weekend morning work is 특근, not 야근. Its cultural foil is the slang 칼퇴 ('knife-exit' = leaving on the dot at quitting time), the thing everyone dreams of instead. And the carrot is 야근 수당 (overtime pay), which is 나오다 (paid out), not 받다-only. The English-speaker pitfall is using 야근 as a blanket word for all 'overtime' — keep the time-of-day nuance — and saying 야근을 가다 ('go to overtime'); you don't go to it, you 야근을 하다.
야근.explanation: "working overtime (late into the night)" is 야근 (yageun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 야근을 하다 ("to work overtime at night"). Watch the particle attached to 야근 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.
야근.shortExplanation: 야근 means "working overtime (late into the night)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 야근 for all overtime — it specifically means working LATE at night; daytime, weekend, or holiday extra work is 특근 or 추가 근무
Saying 야근을 가다 ('go to overtime') — you don't travel to it; the verb is 야근을 하다 (or just 야근해요)
Assuming 야근 수당 is automatic — note the natural opposite 칼퇴 (leaving exactly on time); also overtime pay 나오다 (is paid out) only if the company provides it

usagePhrases.note: the noun takes 하다 for the verb
많다 describes how often it happens
맨날 is casual 'every day', exasperated tone

examples.en: I'm working late again today.
examples.note: simple: 도 'also/again' hints this is a pattern

examples.en: If I work late, do I get overtime pay?
examples.note: everyday: 나오다 'come out (be paid)' is the set verb for 수당

examples.ko: 요즘 프로젝트 때문에 매일 야근해서 너무 피곤해요.
examples.romanization: yojeum peurojekteu ttaemune maeil yageunhaeseo neomu pigonhaeyo.
examples.en: Lately I work late every day because of a project, so I'm exhausted.
examples.note: real situation: 때문에 'because of (a noun)' pins the cause

ex.ko: 메시지는 보내지만 전화는 잘 안 해요.
ex.en: I send messages, but I do not call much.
ex.note: 전화는 contrasts calls with messages.

전화.nuance: 전화 is a noun, but 전화하다 is the verb “to call.”
전화.explanation: 전화 (jeonhwa) = "phone call". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 전화해요 ("I call.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 전화, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
전화.shortExplanation: 전화 means "phone call" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
전화 alone is not a full verb; use 전화해요 or 전화하다 forms.

examples.en: I will call later.
examples.note: Promise.

examples.en: Can you call now?
examples.note: Question.

examples.en: Please call me.
examples.note: Request.

ex.en: Take this medicine after meals.
ex.note: Often paired with a number of minutes.

식후.nuance: 식후 is concise and label-like. In casual speech you can also say 밥 먹고, but at a clinic or pharmacy 식후 is the expected word. 식후 usually pairs with 에 or a time amount: 식후에, 식후 30분.
식후.explanation: "after meals" is 식후 (siku). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 식후에 드세요. ("Take it after meals."). Watch the particle attached to 식후 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.
식후.shortExplanation: 식후 means "after meals" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 식후 for any after-action meaning. It specifically means after meals.
Confusing 식후 with 식전. 식후 is after meals; 식전 is before meals.
Forgetting 에 in speech: 식후에 드세요 is smoother than just 식후 드세요.

usagePhrases.ko: 하루 세 번, 식후에 드셔야 해요.
usagePhrases.romanization: haru se beon, sikue deusyeoya haeyo.
usagePhrases.en: You have to take it three times a day after meals.

examples.ko: 약은 식후에 하루 세 번 드세요.
examples.romanization: yageun sikue haru se beon deuseyo.
examples.en: Take the medicine three times a day after meals.
examples.note: 약 + 식후 + 하루 세 번 is the core pharmacy frame.

ex.ko: 소나기가 갑자기 쏟아지는 바람에 빨래가 다 젖었어요.
ex.en: A downpour came out of nowhere, so all the laundry got soaked.
ex.note: Weather is the purest -는 바람에 cause: sudden and entirely outside your control.

소나기.nuance: 소나기 is a pure native Korean word for a brief, intense burst of rain that arrives and departs suddenly — the classic summer-afternoon downpour. The dividing line from plain 비 is duration and character: 비 is rain in general (steady, all-day, or light), while 소나기 is specifically short-lived and abrupt, so Koreans typically wait it out under an awning rather than buy an umbrella. It contrasts too with 장맛비 (the long monsoon rains) and 이슬비 (drizzle). Natural partners are 내리다/오다, 그치다 (the proper verb for rain stopping — not 끝나다), and 만나다 ('get caught in'). The English-speaker pitfall is using 소나기 for any rain: it must be brief and sudden, and remember it takes the ordinary rain verbs 오다/내리다, with no special verb of its own.
소나기.explanation: 소나기 (sonagi) means "sudden shower". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 소나기가 내리다 ("a sudden shower falls"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 소나기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
소나기.shortExplanation: 소나기 means "sudden shower" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 소나기 for long, steady rain. It specifically means a short, sudden burst; for general or all-day rain say 비.
Saying 소나기가 끝났어요 when the rain stops. Rain 'lets up' with 그치다: 소나기가 그쳤어요.
Forgetting it takes the normal rain verbs. There is no exotic verb — say 소나기가 와요 / 소나기가 내려요, just like 비.

usagePhrases.note: 만나다 idiomatically = run into the rain

examples.en: A sudden shower is coming out of nowhere.
examples.note: simplest form: 갑자기 + 오다 for rain

examples.en: In summer, sudden showers often fall in the afternoon.
examples.note: 자주 = often; describing the seasonal pattern

examples.en: A sudden shower lets up quickly, so just wait a bit.
examples.note: 그치다 + -니까 reasoning; reassuring someone

끊기다.en: to be cut off, to be disconnected

ex.en: The call cuts out when you go into a tunnel.
ex.note: Pronounced [끈키다]. Also used for 연락이 끊기다 (to lose touch).

끊기다.nuance: 끊기다 is passive/intransitive: the video or connection cuts out. 끊다 is what someone actively cuts or ends.
끊기다.explanation: "to cut out; disconnect; buffer" is 끊기다 (kkeunkida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 영상이 계속 끊겨요. ("The video keeps cutting out."). Watch the particle attached to 끊기다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
끊기다.shortExplanation: 끊기다 means "to cut out; disconnect; buffer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 끊다 for a video problem. Say 영상이 끊겨요, not 영상을 끊어요.
Confusing 끊기다 with 느리다. 느리다 is slow; 끊기다 is stopping/cutting out.
Forgetting the subject: 영상이 끊겨요, 와이파이가 끊겨요.

examples.en: The video keeps cutting out, though.
examples.note: -는데요 softly raises the problem.

ex.en: The father put the baby to sleep.
ex.note: Chapter card word-ext-ch57-jaeuda.

재우다.nuance: 자다 is intransitive: 아기가 자요. 재우다 adds a causer: 엄마가 아기를 재워요.
재우다.explanation: "to put someone to sleep" is 재우다 (jaeuda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 아기를 재우다 ("to put a baby to sleep"). Watch the particle attached to 재우다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
재우다.shortExplanation: 재우다 means "to put someone to sleep" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 엄마가 아기를 자요. Use 재우다 when the mother puts the baby to sleep.
Forgetting the object/causee: 아기를 재우다.
Treating 재우다 as simply 'sleep.' The subject is not the sleeper.

usagePhrases.en: to put a baby to sleep
usagePhrases.note: The baby sleeps; someone else causes it.

usagePhrases.en: to put someone to bed early

examples.en: The mother put the baby to sleep.
examples.note: Causative: the baby sleeps, the mother causes it.

웃기다.en: to make someone laugh / to be funny

ex.en: That joke made everyone laugh.
ex.note: Chapter card word-ext-ch57-utgida.

웃기다.nuance: 웃다 is what the person does; 웃기다 is what causes the laughing. In speech, 웃기다 also works like 'to be funny.'
웃기다.explanation: 웃기다 (utgida) = "to make someone laugh; to be funny". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사람들을 웃기다 ("to make people laugh") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 웃기다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
웃기다.shortExplanation: 웃기다 means "to make someone laugh; to be funny" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 웃다 when the subject is the joke. Say 농담이 웃겼어요, not 농담이 웃었어요.
Forgetting that 웃기다 can be casual and colloquial as 'funny.'
Mixing up 웃기다 with 울리다: one causes laughter, the other tears or ringing.

examples.en: That joke made everyone laugh.
examples.note: The joke is the causer.

cluster.title: 재미있다 vs 즐겁다 vs 웃기다
cluster.rule: 재미있다 is the default for anything entertaining or interesting — a movie, a game, a class. 즐겁다 is the pleasant feeling of an activity or time spent together (and the fixed word in wishes like 즐거운 하루 보내세요), while 웃기다 specifically means it makes you laugh.

members.hint: the default "fun / interesting" for things
the pleasant feeling of doing something

members.en: to make someone laugh; to be funny
members.hint: specifically "it makes you laugh"

울리다.en: to make someone cry / to ring

ex.en: That movie made me cry.
ex.note: Chapter card word-ext-ch57-ullida.

울리다.nuance: 울다 is cry or ring by itself; 울리다 makes someone cry or makes a sound ring.
울리다.explanation: 울리다 (ullida) means "to make someone cry; to ring". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 사람을 울리다 ("to make someone cry"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 울리다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
울리다.shortExplanation: 울리다 means "to make someone cry; to ring" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 영화가 울었어요 when the movie made you cry. Say 영화가 저를 울렸어요.
Forgetting the object in emotional causative: 저를/사람들을 울리다.
Confusing 울리다's two uses: emotional 'make cry' and sound 'ring.'

examples.en: That movie made me cry.
examples.note: The film causes the crying.

ex.en: I lowered my voice because we were in a meeting.
ex.note: Chapter card word-ext-ch57-natchuda.

낮추다.nuance: 낮다 is an adjective, while 낮추다 is an action verb. Compare 소리가 낮아요 with 소리를 낮춰 주세요.
낮추다.explanation: "to lower" is 낮추다 (natchuda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 소리를 낮추다 ("to lower the volume"). Watch the particle attached to 낮추다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
낮추다.shortExplanation: 낮추다 means "to lower" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 낮다 as an action: 소리를 낮아요 is wrong. Say 소리를 낮춰요.
Confusing 낮추다 with 내려가다. 내려가다 means go down; 낮추다 means lower something.
Forgetting the object marker: 목소리를 낮추다.

examples.en: I lowered my voice because we were in a meeting.
examples.note: The subject causes the voice level to become lower.

ex.en: The baby wore a coat.
ex.note: Base verb for comparison with 입히다.

입다.nuance: 입다 is a regular verb (입어요, 입었어요, 입습니다) meaning to put on or wear clothing on the torso and legs — shirts, coats, dresses, trousers, uniforms. The thing English speakers must internalize is that Korean has no single verb for 'wear'; it splits the action by body part: 입다 for body clothes, 신다 for footwear (shoes, socks), 쓰다 for things on the head/face (hats, glasses), 끼다 for snug items (gloves, rings), 차다 for things you strap on (watch, belt), and 매다 for ties/scarves you knot. So 'wear shoes' is never 신발을 입다 — it must be 신발을 신다. A second nuance is aspect: 입다 is the action of putting on, while the resulting state 'be wearing' is 입고 있다 (티셔츠를 입고 있어요 = is wearing a T-shirt). The opposite, for taking off any of these, is the single verb 벗다. The pitfall is simply over-extending 입다 to cover everything 'wear' covers in English.
입다.explanation: 입다 (ipda) means "to wear clothes". Start from the polite form 입어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 입다. A strong first sentence is 코트를 입어요 ("I wear a coat"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 입다 also becomes 입고 싶어요 (want), 입을 수 있어요 (can), and 못 입어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
입다.shortExplanation: 입다 means "to wear clothes" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 입다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 입어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 입다 for shoes or socks — footwear takes 신다, so it must be 신발을 신어요, never 신발을 입어요.
Using 입다 for a hat or glasses — head/face items take 쓰다, so 'wear a hat' is 모자를 써요 and 'wear glasses' is 안경을 써요, not 입다.
Saying 옷을 입고 있어요 when you mean the action of getting dressed right now — 입고 있다 is ambiguous toward the state 'am wearing'; to stress the ongoing action of dressing, context or 입는 중이에요 is clearer.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 입다 becomes 입을 수 있어요 ("can") and 입을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: garments worn on the torso/legs take 을/를 with 입다

examples.en: Today I'm wearing warm clothes.
examples.note: weather-driven clothing choice; 옷을 입다 generic

examples.en: I wore a suit because it was a friend's wedding
examples.note: 정장 ('formal suit') is what you wear for special occasions

examples.en: Try this coat on.
examples.note: 입어 보세요 is what a shop clerk says

ex.ko: 영화가 너무 슬퍼서 참다가 울고 말았어요.
ex.en: The film was so sad that I held out and then cried anyway.
ex.note: 울고 말다 is one of the most frequent pairings of this ending.

울다.nuance: 울다 means to cry and is a ㄹ irregular verb: the stem ㄹ drops before endings starting with ㅂ, ㄴ, or ㅅ, so the formal present is 웁니다 (not 울습니다) and the honorific is 우세요; before a plain vowel the ㄹ stays, giving 울어요 and 울었어요, and the future keeps it too in 울 거예요. The crier is the subject and takes 이/가 (아기가 울어요), unlike English where 'cry' can feel transitive. Its natural opposite is 웃다 (laugh), and its near-synonyms split by intensity and register: 눈물을 흘리다 ('shed tears', literally, more composed/quiet) describes tears running down without sobbing, while 흐느끼다 ('to sob') is heavier and more literary; plain 울다 is the everyday all-purpose word, often boosted by mimetics like 펑펑 울다 (bawl) or 엉엉 울다. Note 울다 also describes animals making their cry/call (새가 울다 = a bird sings/cries) and even a phone or alarm 'ringing/sounding'. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation — writing 울습니다 by habit when the ㄹ must drop to 웁니다 — plus confusing 울다 with 웃다, which differ by a single jamo.
울다.explanation: 울다 (ulda) = "to cry". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 울어요 plus one useful sentence like 아기가 울어요 ("the baby cries"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 울고 싶어요 for what you want, 울 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 울어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
울다.shortExplanation: 울다 means "to cry" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 울다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 울어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Keeping the ㄹ before ㅂ and saying 울습니다 — 울다 is ㄹ irregular, so the ㄹ drops there, giving 웁니다 (and the honorific 우세요).
Confusing 울다 (cry) with 웃다 (laugh) — they differ by one jamo, so 울었어요 means 'cried' while 웃었어요 means 'laughed'.
Marking the crier with 을/를 (아기를 울어요) — 울다 is intransitive, so the one crying is the subject: 아기가 울어요 (to MAKE someone cry, use the causative 울리다, as in 동생을 울렸어요).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 울다 becomes 울 수 있어요 ("can") and 울 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem: ㄹ
conjugationTips.body: 울다 is a ㄹ-stem word. The ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ endings: 살다 → 삽니다 (formal), 사는 (describing a noun), 사세요 (honorific). Before a vowel the ㄹ stays: 울어요.

usagePhrases.note: the crier is the subject and takes 이/가

examples.en: The baby often cries at night.
examples.note: subject 아기가; 울어요 keeps ㄹ before a vowel

examples.en: I sobbed watching a sad movie.
examples.note: 펑펑 울다 intensifies; 울었어요 past

examples.en: Don't cry, everything will be okay.
examples.note: 울지 마세요 — ㄹ stays before 지; comforting register

ex.en: I will handle this matter.
ex.note: Linked to dictionary card word-verb-046.

처리하다.nuance: 처리하다 (處理하다, 處 'manage/place' + 理 'put in order') is a workhorse meaning to process, handle, or take care of a task, request, or problem, and the passive 처리되다 ('be processed') saturates official status messages. The register is neutral-professional, ideal for office work and paperwork. Watch three near-neighbors: 해결하다 ('to solve/resolve') implies fully fixing a problem so it's gone, whereas 처리하다 can just mean 'deal with / move it along the pipeline' without a happy ending; 다루다 means 'to handle/treat' in the sense of how you manage a topic or object; and bare 하다 ('do') cannot stand in for 'take care of a matter.' The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that bare-하다 trap: 'I'll do this issue' translated literally as '이 문제를 할게요' is wrong — you must say 처리할게요. Reach for 처리하다 whenever English would say 'handle,' 'take care of,' or 'process.'
처리하다.explanation: 처리하다 (cheorihada) means "to process / to handle / to deal with". Start from the polite form 처리해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 처리하다. A strong first sentence is 업무를 처리하다 ("to handle work tasks"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 처리하다 also becomes 처리하고 싶어요 (want), 처리할 수 있어요 (can), and 처리할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then bend it.
처리하다.shortExplanation: 처리하다 means "to process / to handle / to deal with" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 처리하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 처리해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Learners overuse 하다 alone; '이 문제를 할게요' is wrong. Use 처리하다 to mean 'handle/take care of' a matter.
처리하다 (deal with/move along) isn't always 해결하다 (fully solve). If the issue is actually resolved, say 해결됐어요, not just 처리됐어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 처리하다 becomes 처리할 수 있어요 ("can") and 처리할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I process / to handle / to deal with.
I do not process / to handle / to deal with.
I want to process / to handle / to deal with.
I can process / to handle / to deal with.
I have to process / to handle / to deal with.

usagePhrases.note: Covers processing paperwork, requests, and getting things done.

examples.en: Once the application is received, it is processed within 3 days.
examples.note: Passive 처리되다 in official notices; pairs with 접수되다.

examples.en: I'll handle this issue.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ게요 = speaker's promise; reassuring at work.

examples.ko: 고객 불만이 들어오면 바로 처리해야 해요.
examples.romanization: gogaek bulmani deureoomyeon baro cheorihaeya haeyo.
examples.en: When a customer complaint comes in, you have to deal with it immediately.
examples.note: 불만 = complaint; -아야 해요 = obligation.

ex.en: There are times when you have to decline politely.
ex.note: Linked to dictionary card word-verb-077.

거절하다.nuance: 거절하다 (Sino-Korean 拒絶, 'block-and-sever') is the standard verb for declining a request, offer, or invitation, and the thing refused — 부탁, 제안, 초대 — takes 을/를. Compare it with the harsher 거부하다 (拒否, 'block-and-deny'): 거부하다 is a flat, often institutional rejection ('출석을 거부하다', 'refuse to comply'), while 거절하다 is the ordinary interpersonal 'no thanks'. Because directly refusing can feel rude in Korean social life, 거절하다 is habitually cushioned with 죄송하지만 ('sorry, but…'), 정중하게 ('politely'), or 어렵겠어요 ('that would be difficult'); the bare verb can sound cold. A frequent English-speaker slip is reaching for 거절하다 to mean 'reject a person' romantically — that is 차다 (dump) or 까이다 (get rejected), not 거절하다, which targets the request, not the human. Also do not confuse it with 사양하다, a humble 'I'll pass' used to politely decline an offer of food or a gift.
거절하다.explanation: "to refuse / decline" in Korean is 거절하다 (geojeolha-da). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 거절해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 거절하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 부탁을 거절했어요. ("I turned down the request.") — then reshape the same stem into 거절하고 싶어요 (desire), 거절할 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 거절해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
거절하다.shortExplanation: 거절하다 means "to refuse / decline" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 거절하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 거절해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Do not confuse 거절하다 (decline a request/offer) with the stronger 거부하다, which feels like a flat, often official rejection.
거절하다 takes the offer as its object (제안을 거절하다); to 'reject' a person romantically Koreans say 차다 / 까이다, not 거절하다.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 거절하다 becomes 거절할 수 있어요 ("can") and 거절할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

examples.en: I politely declined the dinner invitation.
examples.note: Note the polite-softening adverb before the verb

examples.en: It feels awkward to turn down the company dinner.
examples.note: 눈치 보이다 = feel socially uncomfortable

examples.en: If it is too much, you can say no.
examples.note: 거절해도 돼요 = giving permission to refuse

ex.en: Eoryeopgesseumnida is often used in courteous refusals.
ex.note: Linked to dictionary card word-ext-1792.

정중하다.nuance: 정중하다 (鄭重하다; the 重 carries 'weighty/grave,' so the word evokes treating someone with weighty respect) means courteous and respectful in a formal, dignified way — proper manners and respectful language. The near-synonym you must separate is 친절하다 (kind/friendly), and the dividing line is warmth vs. form: 친절하다 is personal warmth and helpfulness (a 친절한 점원 smiles and helps you happily), while 정중하다 is formal respect shown through correct manners and language (a 정중한 점원 is impeccably proper, not necessarily warm). For a careful apology, a polite refusal, or staff toward an important guest, you reach for 정중하다, where 친절하다 would feel too casual-warm. Also distinguish 겸손하다 (inner humility about oneself) from 정중하다 (outward courtesy toward others) — different directions. Register: 정중하다 is itself a formal-leaning word, at home in business Korean and written apologies (정중히 사과드립니다). The English-speaker pitfall is collapsing all 'polite' into one word: friendly-polite is 친절하다, formally-courteous is 정중하다. Stem note: 정중해요, not 정중하해요.
정중하다.explanation: "courteous, polite, respectful (in manner)" is 정중하다 (jeongjunghada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 정중하게 부탁하다 ("ask politely/respectfully"). Watch the particle attached to 정중하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
정중하다.shortExplanation: 정중하다 means "courteous, polite, respectful (in manner)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping it with 친절하다 (warm, friendly kindness): 정중하다 is formal respect/courtesy shown through manners
Saying 정중하해요: the 하다 stem gives 정중해요 / 정중한 / 정중하게
Confusing it with 겸손하다: 겸손 is humility about yourself, 정중 is courtesy directed at others

usagePhrases.note: 정중하게 = adverb; signals formal courtesy, a notch above casual 친절
Valued in service and business settings toward customers or clients
Softening a refusal with formal courtesy so it doesn't offend
정중히 = formal -히 adverb; 사과드리다 = humbly apologize — standard in written apologies

examples.en: That person is always courteous.
examples.note: Basic frame; 정중하다 → 정중해요, describing dignified, respectful manners

examples.en: I appreciated the offer but declined politely.
examples.note: Everyday: 제안 = proposal; 정중하게 거절 = a graceful, face-saving no

examples.ko: 고객에게는 이메일을 정중한 표현으로 써야 해요.
examples.romanization: gogaegegeneun imeireul jeongjunghan pyohyeoneuro sseoya haeyo.
examples.en: You must write emails to clients using courteous expressions.
examples.note: Real business situation: 표현 = expression; 정중한 표현 = formal, respectful wording

ex.en: I will help the customer right away.
ex.note: Linked to dictionary card word-ext-140.

손님.nuance: 손님 is native Korean — 손 'guest' + the honorific suffix -님 — so it builds 'guest' into a respectful form, and it covers BOTH a paying customer in a shop AND a guest visiting your home. That built-in 님 is why 손님 is inherently polite and why staff address you directly as 손님 (like English 'sir/ma'am'). Contrast it with the neutral 사람 'person' (too plain and even rude to call a customer) and with 고객, the more formal/corporate term banks, telecoms, and notices use (고객님, 고객 센터 customer center) — 손님 feels face-to-face and shop-floor, 고객 feels institutional. Because 손님 deserves respect, it's counted with the honorific 분 (손님 한 분, not 한 명) and described with honorific verbs (오시다 'come', 계시다 'be present', 기다리고 계세요). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 사람 ('a person came to the shop' → 사람이 왔어요 sounds cold); say 손님이 오셨어요. Collocations: 손님을 받다 (take/receive customers), 손님이 들다 (customers come in), 단골손님 (regular), 손님 접대 (hosting guests).
손님.explanation: "customer" is 손님 (sonnim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 손님이 많아요 ("there are many customers"). Watch the particle attached to 손님 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.
손님.shortExplanation: 손님 means "customer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 사람 instead of 손님 for a customer or guest. 사람이 왔어요 ('a person came') sounds blunt; in a shop or home, say 손님이 왔어요/오셨어요 to show due respect.
Counting customers with 명 instead of the honorific 분. Say 손님 두 분, not 손님 두 명 — 분 raises the politeness that 손님 implies.
Treating 손님 and 고객 as identical in tone. Use 손님 face-to-face in shops and homes; use 고객(님) for formal/written/corporate contexts like 고객 센터 (customer service center).

usagePhrases.note: 많다 'be many'; subject 이 after a consonant
분 is the honorific counter for people, raising respect
모시다 is the humble verb for serving a respected person

examples.en: There are a lot of customers in the shop today.
examples.note: simple: 에 marks the location, 많아요 'are many'

examples.ko: 손님 한 분이 입구에서 기다리고 계세요.
examples.romanization: sonnim han buni ipgueseo gidarigo gyeseyo.
examples.en: One customer is waiting at the entrance.
examples.note: everyday: honorific 분 + 계시다 to respectfully describe the customer

examples.en: Sir/Ma'am, would you come this way?
examples.note: real situation: 손님 used as a direct address term by staff, with honorific -시-

ex.en: I will check the order right away.
ex.note: Linked to dictionary card word-ext-587.

주문.nuance: 주문 is the noun 'order', from 注文 (注 'pour/note down' + 文 'writing') — originally 'to write down a request', which fits ordering perfectly. The verb is 주문하다, and a key contrast is 주문하다 vs 시키다: both mean 'to order', but 시키다 is more casual and also means 'to make someone do something', so toward staff the cleaner, slightly more standard choice is 주문하다 (시키다 is fine among friends: '뭐 시킬까?'). Knowing the bare noun unlocks the phrases you hear constantly — '주문 도와드릴게요', '주문 들어갔어요', '주문 확인해 주세요' — where 주문 stands alone. Register is neutral and identical in casual and formal dining. It collocates with 하다, 들어가다 (go in), 받다 (take an order), 확인하다 (confirm), and 취소하다 (cancel).
주문.explanation: "an order (of food/drink)" is 주문 (jumun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 주문하시겠어요? ("Are you ready to order?"). Watch the particle attached to 주문 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.
주문.shortExplanation: 주문 means "an order (of food/drink)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 주문 (an order) with 주말 (weekend) — they look similar to beginners but are unrelated; mis-saying one for the other changes the meaning entirely.
Defaulting to 시키다 with staff ('이거 시켜 주세요') — understandable but a touch blunt; '이거 주문할게요' or simply '이거 주세요' sounds cleaner to servers.
Treating 주문 as a verb on its own ('주문 주세요') — you need 주문하다, e.g. '주문할게요', or attach 하다.

usagePhrases.note: The staff's standard opening question (honorific 하시-)
Polite phrasing staff use when approaching the table
들어가다 ('go in') = the kitchen has received it
취소되다 (be cancelled); useful if you change your mind fast

examples.en: I'd like to order.
examples.note: The simplest way to flag that you're ready

examples.ko: 주문 아직 안 했어요. 조금만 더 볼게요.
examples.romanization: jumun ajik an haesseoyo. jogeumman deo bolgeyo.
examples.en: We haven't ordered yet. We'll look a bit more.
examples.note: Buys time when staff come too early; 아직 = 'not yet'

examples.en: Since it's a big group, the order all went in at once.
examples.note: 한꺼번에 = 'all at once'; links naturally to 단체

ex.en: I will wait a little.
ex.note: Linked to dictionary card word-ext-1286.

조금.nuance: 조금 means 'a little / a bit / a few' and is the natural counterweight to 많이 for small amounts or mild degrees. Its closest relative is its own contracted form 좀: 조금 is the full, slightly more careful version you can write and say, while 좀 is the quick spoken reduction (조금만요 ↔ 좀만요 are the same idea). Compared with the noun-ish 약간 ('slightly', a touch more formal/written), 조금 is the warm conversational choice. It naturally collocates with quantities and gentle states — 조금 더 ('a little more'), 조금 있다가 ('in a little while') — and its softness makes it ideal for modest answers and polite requests. The English-speaker pitfall is hearing 좀 in speech and not realizing it is just 조금 reduced, and over-stacking it with big-amount words: 조금 많이 is self-contradictory because 조금 only ever points to a small degree.
조금.explanation: 조금 (jogeum) means "a little, a bit, a few". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 조금 주세요 ("Please give me a little"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 조금 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
조금.shortExplanation: 조금 means "a little, a bit, a few" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Not recognizing that 조금 usually contracts to 좀 in casual speech; both are correct, but learners who only study 조금 get lost when they hear 좀.
Pairing 조금 with large amounts: 조금 많이 contradicts itself; 조금 is strictly a small degree, so use 많이 or 너무 for big quantities.
Confusing 조금 with 잠깐/잠시 for time: 조금만 means a small amount, while 잠깐만 specifically means 'for a short moment' of time.

usagePhrases.note: The exact opposite of 많이; requests a small amount
Before an adjective it softens the degree to 'a bit'
조금만 기다려 주세요 = please wait just a moment; 만 ('only') caps it small
A fixed time phrase meaning 'a moment ago'

examples.en: I speak a little Korean.
examples.note: The perfect modest answer for a beginner; 조금 lowers the claim

examples.en: I drank a little water.
examples.note: 조금 before the verb marks a small quantity of the object

examples.en: I'm a little tired today.
examples.note: 조금 softens 피곤하다 so you don't overstate it

cluster.title: 조금 vs 좀 vs 약간
cluster.rule: For real amounts all three overlap — 좀 is simply the spoken contraction of 조금, and 약간 is the cooler, more written "slightly". The deciding fact is that only 좀 has a second life as a request softener, where it means "please / if you would" and not "a little" at all (물 좀 주세요).

members.en: a little, a bit, a few
members.hint: the full form — speech and writing alike
spoken 조금 — and the "please" softener

example.en: Could I get some water, please?

members.hint: the cooler, more written "slightly"

ex.ko: 미리 말했더라면 문제가 커지지 않았을 거예요.
ex.en: If I had said it in advance, the problem would not have gotten bigger.
ex.note: 미리 naturally pairs with 알다, 말하다, 준비하다, and 예약하다.

미리.nuance: 미리 means doing something ahead of the relevant moment so you're ready when it arrives — its whole focus is the timing being early relative to a deadline or event. The classic English-speaker trap is confusing it with 우선 / 먼저 / 일단: 먼저 and 우선 mean 'first in a sequence or in priority' (do A before B), while 미리 means 'before the due time' (do it now so it's done early). 'I paid first' = 먼저 냈어요 (before others), but 'I paid in advance' = 미리 냈어요 (before the due date) — different ideas entirely. 미리 is native Korean, not Sino-Korean, and it glues onto preparation verbs: 미리 예약하다, 미리 준비하다, 미리 확인하다, 미리 알리다. Register is neutral and works in both polite and casual speech. Note the affectionate doubled 미리미리, which nags 'do it good and early.'
미리.explanation: 미리 (miri) means "in advance, ahead of time, beforehand". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 미리 예약하다 ("to book in advance"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 미리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
미리.shortExplanation: 미리 means "in advance, ahead of time, beforehand" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 미리 for 'firstly in a sequence': 미리 이거부터 해요 is odd; for ordering steps you want 우선/먼저 이거부터 해요. 미리 only means 'ahead of the due time.'
Dropping it where the early timing is the point: 예약했어요 alone just says 'I booked'; 미리 예약했어요 adds the crucial 'ahead of time' nuance.
Saying 미리 전에 (advance + before) as a redundant pair under the influence of English 'beforehand in advance'; 미리 already contains 'before,' so just 미리 준비했어요.

usagePhrases.note: The single most useful collocation for residents; pairs with 식당, 호텔, 병원

usagePhrases.en: to say ahead of time / give notice
usagePhrases.note: Used for advance notice; 미리 말해 주세요 = please tell me beforehand
The default verb after 미리; 서류를 미리 준비하다 = prep documents early

usagePhrases.en: well in advance, in good time
usagePhrases.note: Doubled form stressing 'nice and early, with margin to spare'

examples.en: I bought the tickets in advance.
examples.note: Simplest frame: 미리 + buy, the early-action core meaning

examples.ko: 인기 식당은 미리 예약하지 않으면 자리가 없어요.
examples.romanization: ingi sikdangeun miri yeyakaji aneumyeon jariga eopseoyo.
examples.en: Popular restaurants have no seats unless you reserve in advance.
examples.note: Everyday: 미리 + 예약하다 in a -지 않으면 conditional, a real dining reality

examples.ko: 다음 주에 휴가 쓸 거니까 팀장님께 미리 말씀드렸어요.
examples.romanization: daeum jue hyuga sseul geonikka timjangnimkke miri malsseumdeuryeosseoyo.
examples.en: I'll take leave next week, so I gave my team lead a heads-up in advance.
examples.note: Real situation: 미리 + 말씀드리다 (humble form) for workplace advance notice

ex.ko: 화가 나서 다 말해 버렸는데 지금은 후회해요.
ex.en: I was angry and blurted it all out, and now I regret it.
ex.note: The regret reading of -아/어 버리다 often gets spelled out this way.

후회하다.nuance: 후회하다 is Sino-Korean — 後悔 literally stacks 後 'after' + 悔 'regret/remorse', i.e. the regret that comes AFTER the deed — and names the painful wish that you had chosen differently. It typically points backward (그 결정을 후회해요 'I regret that decision') and frequently pairs with a reason clause in -아서/어서 or with a past-action nominalizer -(으)ㄴ 걸: 그렇게 말한 걸 후회해. Distinguish it from 아쉽다, which is a milder 'it's a shame / I wish it were a bit different' about things often outside your control, whereas 후회하다 carries genuine self-reproach over your own past action. Also separate it from 미안하다 ('to be sorry' TO someone) — 후회하다 is regret felt inside, not an apology directed at another person. Pitfall: 'I regret to inform you' has no 후회하다 equivalent; that polite-letter formula becomes 안타깝게도 or 죄송하지만. Keep the object with 를, and remember the negative splits as 후회 안 해요.
후회하다.explanation: "to regret" in Korean is 후회하다 (huhoehada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 후회해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 후회하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 후회 안 해요 ("I have no regrets") — then reshape the same stem into 후회하고 싶어요 (desire), 후회할 수 있어요 (ability), and 후회할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
후회하다.shortExplanation: 후회하다 means "to regret" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 후회하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 후회해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 후회하다 as an apology to someone: 너한테 후회해. To apologize you need 미안하다/죄송하다 (미안해); 후회하다 is internal regret, not 'sorry to you'.
Confusing it with mild 아쉽다. 'It's a shame the trip ended' = 여행이 끝나서 아쉬워요; deep self-blame over your decision = 그 결정을 후회해요.
Saying 후회를 안 해요 awkwardly in speech — fine, but the more idiomatic split is 후회 안 해요, and 'I'll regret it' is 후회할 거예요, not 후회겠어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 후회하다 becomes 후회할 수 있어요 ("can") and 후회할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Firm, often defiant statement (noun split by 안)

examples.en: I regret that choice
examples.note: Object + 를; the thing you regret

examples.en: I regretted talking too much
examples.note: -아서 gives the reason for the regret

examples.ko: 지금 안 하면 나중에 후회할 거야
examples.romanization: jigeum an hamyeon najunge huhoehal geoya
examples.en: If you don't do it now, you'll regret it later
examples.note: Casual; conditional 면 + future warning

ex.ko: 그때 말하지 않은 게 아직도 후회예요.
ex.en: Not saying it back then is still a regret.
ex.note: Noun form 후회 works when the regret itself is the topic.

후회.nuance: 후회 is regret aimed squarely *backward* at a choice you already made, with a sting of self-blame. It is Sino-Korean 後悔 (後 'after/behind' + 悔 'to repent'), literally 'after-regret', the regret that comes *after* the deed. The verb 후회하다 is everyday, but the noun surfaces in lines like 후회예요 or 후회가 남아요, and the motto 후회 없이 (without regret) is hugely popular among 20-30s. The key synonym contrast is 후회 vs 아쉬움: 후회 blames *your own* decision ('I shouldn't have done that'), while 아쉬움 is a softer, fate-tinged 'aw, what a shame it didn't work out' with little self-blame. The English-speaker trap is mapping 'I regret it' straight to 후회해요 when you actually want the noun-predicate 후회예요 ('it's a regret'), and reaching for 후회 when the gentle 아쉬움 is what the situation calls for.
후회.explanation: 후회 (huhoe) = "regret". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 후회하다 ("to regret") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 후회, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
후회.shortExplanation: 후회 means "regret" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 후회 with 아쉬움. 후회 carries self-blame over a choice you made; 아쉬움 is the gentler 'too bad / what a shame' with no blame. Telling a friend 후회되겠다 can sound like you're saying it was their fault.
Saying 후회해요 when you mean 'it's a regret.' For the noun-predicate use 후회예요 (or 후회가 돼요); 후회해요 is the verb 'I (actively) regret.'
Using 후회 for forward-looking worry. Regret only looks back at the past; for 'I'm worried it might go wrong' use 걱정 instead.

usagePhrases.note: the verb; 후회 itself is the noun, so for the action use 후회하다
the feeling wells up on its own; slightly passive, less self-blaming than 후회하다
the motto phrase: 후회 없이 살자, 후회 없이 도전하다
set idiom (lit. 'beat the ground and regret') for deep, too-late regret

examples.ko: 지금 안 사면 나중에 후회할 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: jigeum an samyeon najunge huhoehal geot gatayo.
examples.en: If I don't buy it now, I think I'll regret it later.
examples.note: Simple future hunch: 후회하다 + -ㄹ 것 같다 = 'I think I'll regret'; points forward to a choice not yet made.

examples.ko: 그때 그 집 계약 안 한 게 두고두고 후회예요.
examples.romanization: geuttae geu jip gyeyak an han ge dugodugo huhoeyeyo.
examples.en: I keep regretting not signing the lease on that place back then.
examples.note: Noun-as-predicate 후회예요; 두고두고 = 'over and over, lingeringly,' a perfect partner for regret.

examples.en: I want to give it a real try, with no regrets.
examples.note: 후회 없이 = the regret-free mindset phrase young Koreans love as a life motto.

ex.ko: 그 기회를 잡았더라면 다른 회사에 갔을지도 몰라요.
ex.en: If I had taken that opportunity, I might have gone to a different company.
ex.note: 기회를 잡다 and 기회를 놓치다 are both useful in hindsight.

기회.nuance: 기회 (機會, 機 'opportune moment/device' + 會 'meeting') is a window of opportunity that may not come twice, so it carries a faint pressure to act. The key contrast is 기회 vs 기능: 기회 is a chance to do something, while 기능 is a 'function/feature.' Koreans treat 기회 as something you physically handle — 기회를 잡다 (seize), 기회를 놓치다 (miss), 기회를 주다/얻다 (give/get) — so the partner verb is concrete, never 기회를 하다. With existence it is 기회가 있다/없다, and 기회가 되면 is a gentle, non-committal 'if the chance comes up.' The English-speaker trap is twofold: don't say 기회를 하다 by mapping 'take a chance' word-for-word, and don't mark existence with 를 (기회를 있다 ✗ → 기회가 있다 ✓). Register is neutral, fine in both polite speech and writing.
기회.explanation: 기회 (gihoe) = "chance; opportunity". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 기회가 있어요 ("there is a chance") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기회, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
기회.shortExplanation: 기회 means "chance; opportunity" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 기회를 하다 by translating 'take a chance' literally — the verb is 기회를 잡다 (seize) or 기회를 얻다 (get)
Marking existence with 를: 기회를 있다 ✗. Existence always takes 가: 기회가 있다 ✓
Treating 기회 like 기능 (function/feature); they share 기 but mean different things

usagePhrases.note: existence takes 가, never 를: 기회가 있다
잡다 (grab) is the default verb, not 하다
좋은 modifies the noun directly, no 의
set phrase for a soft, open-ended offer

examples.en: Is there a chance?
examples.note: simplest existence frame with 가 있다

examples.ko: 저는 외국에서 일할 기회를 잡고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun oegugeseo ilhal gihoereul japgo sipeoyo.
examples.en: I want to seize a chance to work abroad.
examples.note: a verb + ㄹ 기회 = 'a chance to do X'

examples.ko: 좋은 기회였는데 그때 안 잡아서 지금도 아쉬워요.
examples.romanization: joeun gihoeyeonneunde geuttae an jabaseo jigeumdo aswiwoyo.
examples.en: It was a good opportunity, but I didn't take it then, so I still regret it.
examples.note: real-talk: 기회를 잡다/놓치다 in past reflection

ex.ko: 먼저 사과했더라면 아직 어색하지 않았을 텐데요.
ex.en: If I had apologized first, it would not still be awkward.
ex.note: 사과했더라면 fits relationship repair after the fact.

사과하다.nuance: 사과하다 is 謝過(사과)하다, hanja 謝 'express thanks/apology' + 過 'fault/error', so it literally means to 'acknowledge one's fault' — you take responsibility for a mistake to the person you wronged, who is marked with 에게/한테 or honorific 께. The boundary against 미안하다 and 변명하다 is essential: 미안하다 is the adjective/feeling 'to be sorry' (an emotional state — 미안해요), while 사과하다 is the ACT of formally apologizing (you can 사과하다 even publicly or in writing); and 변명하다 is the opposite move, to 'make excuses.' So you might 사과하다 instead of merely feeling 미안하다. The cause of the apology attaches with -아서: 늦어서 사과했어요. A notorious trap is the homograph: 사과 also means 'apple' (native-Korean noun), so context disambiguates 사과를 했어요 'apologized' from 사과를 먹었어요 'ate an apple' — they share spelling but are unrelated words. English speakers also wrongly say '~에 대해 미안해요' as if 'sorry' were a verb taking objects; to apologize FOR something, use 사과하다 with -아서 or -에 대해. Regular 하다 verb: 사과 + 해요, negative 사과 안 해요.
사과하다.explanation: "to apologize" in Korean is 사과하다 (sagwahada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 사과해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 사과하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 친구에게 사과하다 ("apologize to a friend") — then reshape the same stem into 사과하고 싶어요 (desire), 사과할 수 있어요 (ability), and 사과 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
사과하다.shortExplanation: 사과하다 means "to apologize" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 사과하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 사과해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
