Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 쏟다 also becomes 쏟고 싶어요 (want), 쏟을 수 있어요 (can), and 못 쏟아요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then bend it.
쏟다.shortExplanation: 쏟다 means "to spill" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 쏟다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 쏟아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Spelling the stem wrong: writing 쏟아요 as 쏘다요 or 쏟어요 — the stem is 쏟- and takes 아 (bright vowel ㅗ), giving 쏟아요, 쏟았어요.
Using 쏟다 for a tiny spill: a few drops on your clothes is better said 흘리다 (흘렸어요); 쏟다 implies a large amount poured out at once.
Confusing 쏟다 with 쏟아지다: 'the rain is pouring' is the intransitive 비가 쏟아져요, not 비가 쏟아요 (which would need an actor spilling rain).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 쏟다 becomes 쏟을 수 있어요 ("can") and 쏟을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: to spill water (a lot, at once)
usagePhrases.note: Object takes 를; implies a sizable amount tipping out

examples.en: Oops, I spilled the coffee!
examples.note: Casual exclamation 쏟았어; sudden accident

examples.en: The kid spilled milk all over the table.
examples.note: Surface 식탁에 takes 에; whole-amount spill

examples.en: I poured all my heart into this work.
examples.note: 정성을 쏟다 idiom; 온 'whole' intensifies

ex.ko: 앞사람이 갑자기 멈추는 바람에 넘어질 뻔했어요.
ex.en: The person in front stopped suddenly, so I nearly fell over.
ex.note: Near-misses and -는 바람에 belong together: sudden cause, bad near-outcome.

넘어지다.nuance: 넘어지다 means a standing person (or upright thing) loses balance and topples to the ground, built on 넘다 'to go over' + -어지다 'to come to be', literally 'to come to fall over'. The line to draw is against 떨어지다 ('to fall FROM a height / to drop'): a person on their feet 넘어지다, but a cup off a table or a leaf from a tree 떨어지다 — and against 쓰러지다, which is to collapse from illness/exhaustion (fainting) rather than from tripping. Register is plain and used for everyone. The place where you fall takes 에서 (action location), and the cause is usually chained with -어서: 미끄러져서 넘어졌어요. Natural collocations: 넘어져서 무릎이 까지다 (scrape a knee falling), 넘어질 뻔하다 (almost fall), 넘어지지 않게 조심하다. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 떨어지다 because English uses 'fall' for both — but 'I fell (down)' on flat ground is always 넘어지다; save 떨어지다 for dropping or falling off something.
넘어지다.explanation: 넘어지다 (neomeoji-da) means "to fall down". Start from the polite form 넘어져요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 넘어지다. A strong first sentence is 길에서 넘어지다 ("to fall down on the street"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 넘어지다 also becomes 넘어지고 싶어요 (want), 넘어질 수 있어요 (can), and 못 넘어져요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then bend it.
넘어지다.shortExplanation: 넘어지다 means "to fall down" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 넘어지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 넘어져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 떨어지다 for tripping over on flat ground. A person who trips and goes down says 넘어졌어요; 떨어지다 is for falling FROM a height or an object dropping.
Using 넘어지다 for fainting/collapsing from illness. That is 쓰러지다 (더위 먹고 쓰러졌어요). 넘어지다 implies a trip or loss of footing, not a medical collapse.
Marking the place with 에 instead of 에서. Falling is an action that happens somewhere, so 계단에서 넘어졌어요 (with 에서), not 계단에 넘어졌어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 넘어지다 becomes 넘어질 수 있어요 ("can") and 넘어질 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: to fall down on the street
usagePhrases.note: Place of falling takes 에서, the action location

examples.en: The child fell down.
examples.note: Simplest: subject 이, past tense, no place needed

examples.en: I slipped on the icy road and fell down.
examples.note: Everyday: 미끄러지다 (cause) then 넘어지다 (result), the classic pair

examples.en: Grandmother fell on the stairs and went to the hospital.
examples.note: Real situation: honorific -시- on 넘어지셔서 and 가셨어요 for an elder

지각하다.en: to be late (for school or work)

ex.ko: 알람을 못 듣는 바람에 오늘도 지각했어요.
ex.en: I didn't hear my alarm, so I was late again today.
ex.note: 지각하다 is specifically institutional lateness; 늦다 is the general word.

지각하다.nuance: 지각하다 is Sino-Korean 지각 (遲刻, 'late-moment') + 하다, meaning specifically to arrive late to an appointed place like school, work, or a meeting — it is the institutional 'tardy', the kind a teacher or boss notes. The vital contrast is with the adjective 늦다 ('to be late' in general): 늦다 covers ANY lateness ('the bus is late', 'I'm running late', 늦어서 미안해요), whereas 지각하다 is narrowly being tardy to a fixed obligation. So 'sorry I'm late' to a friend is 늦어서 미안해요, never 지각해서; save 지각하다 for school/office tardiness. Register is neutral-formal, with a school/workplace flavor. The place you're late to takes 에 (회사에 지각하다). As a 하다 verb, the negative and potential split the noun off: 지각 안 해요, 지각 못 해요 — not 안 지각해요. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly using 지각하다 for every 'I'm late', when most casual lateness should be plain 늦다.
지각하다.explanation: 지각하다 (jigakha-da) means "to be late". Start from the polite form 지각해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 지각하다. A strong first sentence is 학교에 지각하다 ("to be late to school"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 지각하다 also becomes 지각하고 싶어요 (want), 지각할 수 있어요 (can), and 지각 못 해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then bend it.
지각하다.shortExplanation: 지각하다 means "to be late" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 지각하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 지각해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 지각하다 for casual lateness to friends: 친구한테 지각했어요 sounds odd. For everyday 'I'm late', use the adjective 늦다: 늦어서 미안해. Reserve 지각하다 for school/work tardiness.
Forming the negative as 안 지각해요. Split the 하다 compound: 지각 안 해요 (and 지각 못 해요 for can-not).
Marking the destination with 에서 instead of 에. You are late ARRIVING somewhere, so 학교에 지각했어요 (with 에), not 학교에서.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 지각하다 becomes 지각할 수 있어요 ("can") and 지각할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: The institution you're late TO takes 에

examples.en: I was late to school.
examples.note: Simplest: institution 학교 + 에, past 지각했어요

examples.en: I overslept so I was late to work.
examples.note: Everyday: cause 늦잠을 자다 'oversleep' + the 하다 verb past

examples.ko: 한 번만 더 지각하면 결석으로 처리돼요.
examples.romanization: han beonman deo jigakamyeon gyeolseogeuro cheoridwaeyo.
examples.en: If you're late just one more time it'll be counted as an absence.
examples.note: Real situation: institutional consequence, 결석 'absence' contrast

ex.ko: 지하철이 멈추는 바람에 그냥 재택근무로 바꿨어요.
ex.en: The subway stopped running, so I just switched to working from home.
ex.note: The outcome here is a fallback, not a good result, so 바람에 still fits.

재택근무.nuance: 재택근무 is the formal term for working from home, very commonly clipped to just 재택 in speech (오늘 재택이에요). It is fully Sino-Korean 在宅勤務, parsing as 在 'be located' + 宅 'home/residence' + 근무 'duty/work' — literally 'home-located work duty'. It exploded into daily vocabulary after COVID, so 재택근무 가능해요? is now a normal thing to ask when job hunting. The synonym field: 재택근무 (at home specifically) sits inside the broader 원격근무 (遠隔, 'remote work' from anywhere), while 외근 (off-site duty) is its near-opposite — leaving to go OUT, not staying in. The English-speaker pitfall is inventing a descriptive phrase like 집에서 근무 or 집에서 일해요 as if it were the term: those describe the activity, but the fixed noun is 재택근무. Also keep it apart from 외근 — both involve not sitting at your assigned office desk, but 재택은 home, 외근 is the field.
재택근무.explanation: 재택근무 (jaetaekgeunmu) means "working from home; remote work". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 재택근무를 하다 ("to work from home"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 재택근무 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.
재택근무.shortExplanation: 재택근무 means "working from home; remote work" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 집에서 근무 as if it were the set term — it merely describes the activity; the established noun is 재택근무 (or clipped 재택)
Confusing it with 외근, which means going OUT for work duties — 재택근무 is staying HOME (在宅)
Saying 재택근무를 가다 ('go to WFH') — you don't go anywhere; use 재택근무를 하다 or 오늘 재택이에요

usagePhrases.note: the noun takes 하다 to become a verb
가능하다 (可能) 'be possible', a job-hunting keyword
주 N회 'N times a week', 재택 is the clipped form

examples.en: I'm working from home today.
examples.note: simple: clipped 재택 + 이에요 in casual speech

examples.en: Our company allows working from home.
examples.note: everyday: 가능해요 frames it as a permitted perk

examples.ko: 재택근무하니까 출퇴근 시간이 없어서 너무 편해요.
examples.romanization: jaetaekgeunmuhanikka chultoegeun sigani eopseoseo neomu pyeonhaeyo.
examples.en: Since I work from home, there's no commute, so it's really comfortable.
examples.note: real situation: 니까 'because/since' gives the reason for the upside

다치다.en: to get hurt, to injure oneself

ex.en: He pushed too hard at the gym, and in the end he hurt his knee.
ex.note: You watched the overtraining, so -더니 carries the whole build-up.

다치다.nuance: 다치다 is the everyday verb for getting physically injured — bumps, cuts, sprains, breaks — and crucially the injured body part takes 을/를, not 이/가 (무릎을 다쳤어요, not 무릎이). Although it translates as 'to hurt', it behaves like an intransitive 'to GET hurt' aimed at yourself, so you cannot use it to mean 'I hurt someone else' — that is 다치게 하다 or 상처를 입히다. The nearest neighbor is 아프다, and the dividing line matters: 다치다 is the one-time event of getting injured (넘어져서 다쳤어요), while 아프다 is the lingering pain or sickness that follows (지금도 아파요). It pairs habitually with 크게 다치다 (badly hurt), 살짝/조금 다치다 (slightly hurt), and 다친 데 (the injured spot). At a hospital, 다치다 plus the exact body part (발목, 허리, 손목) gets you to the right department fast.
다치다.explanation: 다치다 (dachida) means "to get hurt". Start from the polite form 다쳐요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 다치다. A strong first sentence is 어디 다쳤어요? ("Where did you get hurt?"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 다치다 also becomes 다치고 싶어요 (want), 다칠 수 있어요 (can), and 다칠 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then bend it.
다치다.shortExplanation: 다치다 means "to get hurt" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 다치다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 다쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 아프다 when you mean an injury — 아프다 is 'it hurts / I'm sick' (a state), but 다치다 is the act of getting injured (an event). Say '넘어져서 다쳤어요' for the injury, then '지금도 아파요' for the pain that remains.
Marking the body part with 이/가 — it's 무릎을 다쳤어요 (object 을), not 무릎이 다쳤어요. The body part is what you injure, so it takes 을/를.
Trying to say 'I hurt my friend' with 다치다 — 친구를 다쳤어요 is wrong because 다치다 is about getting hurt yourself. Use 친구를 다치게 했어요 ('I caused my friend to get hurt').

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 다치다 becomes 다칠 수 있어요 ("can") and 다칠 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: The first thing people ask if you limp in or hold an injured spot; 어디 = 'where (on the body)'.

examples.en: I hurt my hand.
examples.note: Simplest frame: body part + 을/를 + 다치다. The hurt body part is the object, not the subject.

examples.en: I hurt my knee while playing soccer.
examples.note: V-다가 = 'while doing X, (something happened)'; the most common way to set up how an injury occurred.

examples.ko: 넘어져서 손목을 좀 다쳤는데 병원 가야 할까요?
examples.romanization: neomeojyeoseo sonmogeul jom dachyeonneunde byeongwon gaya halkkayo?
examples.en: I fell and hurt my wrist a bit — should I go to the hospital?
examples.note: Real clinic-decision moment; 넘어지다 = to fall over, and naming 손목 (wrist) routes you to 정형외과 (orthopedics).

ex.ko: 밤늦게까지 보고서를 끝내느라고 한숨도 못 잤어요.
ex.en: I was finishing the report until late at night, so I didn't sleep at all.
ex.note: 끝내다 is transitive ('finish it'); 끝나다 is what the thing itself does.

끝내다.nuance: 끝내다 is the active, everyday verb for finishing or wrapping something up — you make it end. It is the transitive causative of 끝나다: the pair 끝내다 / 끝나다 is the cleanest minimal contrast in the whole 'finish' family, and getting it right is the core skill here. 끝내다 takes an object and means YOU end it (숙제를 끝냈어요 'I finished the homework'); 끝나다 is intransitive and means it ends by itself (수업이 끝났어요 'class ended'). Against 마치다, 끝내다 is the more casual, task-focused choice — perfect for daily office lines like 이것만 끝내고 갈게요 — whereas 마치다 is bookish and ceremonial. (Note 끝내다 also has a slang sense: 끝내주다 / 끝내준다 = 'awesome', literally 'it finishes you off'.) Conjugation is easy and regular: stem 끝내- gives past 끝냈어요. Habitual collocations: 일을 끝내다, 숙제를 끝내다, 빨리 끝내다, 오늘 안에 끝내다.
끝내다.explanation: "to finish (wrap up)" in Korean is 끝내다 (kkeutnaeda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 끝내요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 끝내다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 일을 끝내다 ("to get the work done") — then reshape the same stem into 끝내고 싶어요 (desire), 끝낼 수 있어요 (ability), and 끝낼 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
끝내다.shortExplanation: 끝내다 means "to finish (wrap up)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 끝내다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 끝내요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't swap transitive 끝내다 (you finish it) with intransitive 끝나다 (it finishes): 숙제를 끝냈어요 (object + 끝내다) vs. 수업이 끝났어요 (subject + 끝나다). Saying 수업을 끝났어요 is a classic particle/verb mismatch.
Past tense spelling: it's 끝냈어요 (stem 끝내- + 었), not 끝났어요 — 끝났어요 belongs to 끝나다. Mixing the two stems garbles which verb you mean.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 끝내다 becomes 끝낼 수 있어요 ("can") and 끝낼 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Transitive: 일을 / 숙제를 / 회의를 끝내다 — you actively bring it to an end.

examples.en: Let me just finish this and then go.
examples.note: 만 = 'just this'; -고 갈게요 chains 'finish, then leave'. Very natural daily phrase.

examples.en: I couldn't finish all the work.
examples.note: 못 + 끝내다 = 'couldn't manage to finish'; 다 = all. Past is 끝냈어요 (stem 끝내-).

examples.en: Can we wrap up the meeting within 30 minutes?
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 수 있을까요 = 'do you think we can ~?'; practical scheduling question.

ex.en: I overslept, so I missed the first train.
ex.note: 늦잠을 자다 keeps its 을 even inside -는 바람에.

정신없다.en: to be hectic, to be all over the place

ex.ko: 이사 준비하느라고 이번 주 내내 정신이 없었어요.
ex.en: I was getting ready to move, so I was frazzled all week.
ex.note: 정신이 없다 is the most common result clause after -느라고.

ex.ko: 찬 음식을 많이 먹었더니 배탈이 났어요.
ex.en: I ate a lot of cold food, and I ended up with an upset stomach.
ex.note: 배탈이 나다, like 몸살이 나다, uses 나다 rather than 하다.

지치다.en: to be worn out, to be drained

ex.en: He overdid it for a few days, and now he looks completely drained.
ex.note: 지치다 describes a state you can see, so it sits well in a -더니 result.

ex.ko: 엘리베이터가 고장 나는 바람에 계단으로 올라갔어요.
ex.en: The lift broke down, so I took the stairs up.
ex.note: 고장 나다 (it breaks) and 고장 내다 (you break it) are worth keeping apart.

버리다.en: to throw away; (auxiliary) to do completely

ex.en: I deleted all the old photos.
ex.note: As an auxiliary, -아/어 버리다 means the action went right through to the end.

버리다.nuance: 버리다 means to discard something as no longer wanted — to throw it out as trash or to abandon it. Don't confuse it with 던지다, which is to throw an object through the air toward a target (공을 던지다 'throw a ball'); 버리다 is about getting rid of, not about the flying motion. A second hugely important use is as an auxiliary verb -아/어 버리다, which colors the main verb with 'completely' or 'regrettably/finally': 잊어버리다 'forget (clean out of mind)', 가 버리다 '(someone) just left'. So a learner must read context: 버려요 alone = throw away, but 먹어 버려요 = eat it all up. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 던지다 whenever they see 'throw' — but 'throw away/out' in the disposal sense is always 버리다. Also note Korea's strict 분리수거 (recycling separation) culture, so 버리다 in daily life often pairs with sorting.
버리다.explanation: "to throw away" in Korean is 버리다 (beorida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 버려요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 버리다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 쓰레기를 버리다 ("to throw away trash") — then reshape the same stem into 버리고 싶어요 (desire), 버릴 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 버려요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
버리다.shortExplanation: 버리다 means "to throw away" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 버리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 버려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 던지다 for disposal (쓰레기를 던지다) — that means hurling the trash through the air; to dispose of it you must say 쓰레기를 버리다.
Misreading the auxiliary: hearing 다 써 버렸어요 as 'threw away while writing' — here 버리다 is auxiliary meaning 'used it all up'; the real main verb is 쓰다.
Forgetting that 버리다 also means 'abandon (a person)' (애인을 버리다) — so in emotional contexts it can sound harsh; don't use it lightly about people.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 버리다 becomes 버릴 수 있어요 ("can") and 버릴 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: The most basic collocation; 쓰레기 'garbage' is the prototypical object

examples.en: Is it okay to throw this away?
examples.note: -아도 돼요 asks permission before discarding something

examples.en: I threw out all the clothes I don't wear.
examples.note: Topic 옷은 sets 'as for clothes'; 다 'all' shows total disposal

examples.en: It's still usable, so please don't throw it away.
examples.note: -ㄹ 만하다 'worth doing' justifies keeping it

ex.en: I held out to the very end, and then broke down anyway.
ex.note: 참다 supplies exactly the resistance that -고 말다 requires.

참다.nuance: 참다 is a native verb meaning to ENDURE, BEAR, or HOLD BACK — both physical discomfort (아픔을 참다 'endure pain') and inner urges you suppress (화를 참다 'hold back anger', 눈물을 참다 'hold back tears', 웃음을 참다 'stifle a laugh'). The stem ends in ㅁ, so it is a REGULAR verb: add 아 → 참아요, past 참았어요 — never 참어요 (the bright ㅏ vowel governs the ending). Contrast it with 견디다, which is to withstand a prolonged hardship or pressure over time (고통을 견디다 'endure suffering', 더위를 견디다 'bear the heat'); 참다 leans toward actively restraining a momentary impulse, while 견디다 leans toward holding up under sustained strain. 참다 carries cultural weight — patience and self-restraint (참을성) are prized virtues. Pitfall: choose 참아요 not 참어요, and for an ongoing battle against hardship 견디다 often fits better than 참다.
참다.explanation: 참다 (chamda) means "to endure". Start from the polite form 참아요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 참다. A strong first sentence is 조금만 참아요 ("Hold on just a little"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 참다 also becomes 참고 싶어요 (want), 참을 수 있어요 (can), and 참을 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
참다.shortExplanation: 참다 means "to endure" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 참다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 참아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Conjugating it as 참어요. The stem vowel ㅏ is bright, so it takes 아: 참아요, past 참았어요.
Using 참다 for long-term withstanding: 일 년 동안 참았어요 for 'endured for a year' is better as 견뎠어요. 참다 = restrain a momentary urge; 견디다 = hold up under sustained hardship.
Forgetting 못 for the 'can't bear it' meaning: saying 안 참아요 ('I choose not to endure') when you mean 못 참아요 ('I can't endure it'). 못 marks inability.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 참다 becomes 참을 수 있어요 ("can") and 참을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: 조금만 = just a bit; encouragement to bear with it

examples.en: I held back my anger
examples.note: 화를 참다 = suppress anger, a very common pairing

examples.en: I have to endure the pain
examples.note: 아픈 걸 = 아픈 것을, 'the painful thing'

examples.en: I couldn't hold back my laughter
examples.note: Casual past; 웃음 = laughter, with the cannot form

ex.en: I very nearly forgot our plans.
ex.note: One of the lexicalized 버리다 verbs — written as a single word.

잊어버리다.nuance: 잊어버리다 is the native compound 잊다 ('forget') + -어 버리다 (the auxiliary 버리다, 'throw away / do completely'), so it means to forget thoroughly, with the nuance that the memory is gone for good — often tinged with regret ('darn, it's gone'). Plain 잊다 states the bare fact of forgetting; 잊어버리다 adds finality and emotional color, which is why everyday speech overwhelmingly uses 잊어버리다. The object takes 을/를. Conjugation: the 리 stem contracts with 어 to 려, hence 잊어버려요 / 잊어버렸어요. The most dangerous English-speaker pitfall is the near-twin 잃어버리다 ('to lose a physical object'): 잊다 (forget, from the mind) vs 잃다 (lose, from your possession) differ by one jamo and one meaning — you 잊어버리다 a name but 잃어버리다 your wallet. Mixing them is the classic learner error. Also note: to tell someone 'don't forget', say 잊어버리지 마세요 or just 잊지 마세요; and writing the uncontracted 잊어버리었어요 is wrong — it must be 잊어버렸어요.
잊어버리다.explanation: "to forget" in Korean is 잊어버리다 (ijeobeorida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 잊어버려요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 잊어버리다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 이름을 잊어버리다 ("to forget a name") — then reshape the same stem into 잊어버리고 싶어요 (desire), 잊어버릴 수 있어요 (ability), and 잊어버릴 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
잊어버리다.shortExplanation: 잊어버리다 means "to forget" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 잊어버리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 잊어버려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing it with 잃어버리다 ('lose an object'). You 잊어버리다 information (이름을 잊어버렸어요) but 잃어버리다 things (지갑을 잃어버렸어요). One jamo, totally different meaning.
Writing the uncontracted past 잊어버리었어요. The 리 + 었 contracts to 렸: 잊어버렸어요.
Thinking 잊다 and 잊어버리다 are fully interchangeable. 잊어버리다 adds 'completely/for good' and is the everyday choice; bare 잊다 is more neutral or literary.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 잊어버리다 becomes 잊어버릴 수 있어요 ("can") and 잊어버릴 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Object + 을/를 + 잊어버리다; 약속을 잊어버리다 ('forget an appointment') is a common slip.

examples.en: I forgot the password
examples.note: Everyday frame; note the past 리 + 었 → 렸: 잊어버렸어요.

examples.en: It slipped my mind and I didn't bring an umbrella
examples.note: 깜빡 잊어버리고 ('forgetting in a flash, and...') chains to the consequence.

examples.en: Please forget all the bad memories
examples.note: 잊어버리세요 ('do forget') used kindly to help someone move on.

ex.en: I was careful, and the cup still ended up broken.
ex.note: 깨지다 takes 이/가 (it breaks); the transitive 깨다 takes 을/를.

깨지다.nuance: 깨지다 is the verb for hard, brittle things shattering or cracking — glass, dishes, phone screens, eggs — and the key is matching the verb to the material: it contrasts with 부러지다 (long, rigid things snapping: 팔이/연필이 부러지다) and 찢어지다 (paper or fabric tearing: 종이가/옷이 찢어지다). Figuratively it covers promises, deals, records, and moods 'breaking' (약속이/기록이/분위기가 깨지다), and in casual speech 둘이 깨졌어 means a couple split up. It's intransitive (the broken thing takes 이/가); to smash something yourself, use the transitive 깨다 (컵을 깼어요 = I broke the cup) — note the e/ae spelling difference, 깨다 vs 깨지다. The 요-form is 깨져요 (지 + 어 → 져). English speakers habitually say 'I broke the glass' with the intransitive form; you must use 깨다 when there's an agent.
깨지다.explanation: 깨지다 (kkaejida) means "to break, to shatter, to fall through". Start from the polite form 깨져요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 깨지다. A strong first sentence is 컵이 떨어져서 깨졌어요. ("The cup fell and broke."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 깨지다 also becomes 깨지고 싶어요 (want), 깨질 수 있어요 (can), and 깨질 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
깨지다.shortExplanation: 깨지다 means "to break, to shatter, to fall through" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 깨지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 깨져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use it transitively — say 유리가 깨졌어요 (the glass broke), but 유리를 깼어요 when YOU broke it (깨다).
Match the verb to the material: glass/ceramics 깨지다, sticks/bones 부러지다, paper/clothes 찢어지다.
Don't confuse the spellings — 깨다 (transitive, 'break/smash') vs 깨지다 (intransitive, 'get broken'); the 지 marks the passive-ish 'happens to it' meaning.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 깨지다 becomes 깨질 수 있어요 ("can") and 깨질 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I break, to shatter, to fall through.
I do not break, to shatter, to fall through.
I want to break, to shatter, to fall through.
I can break, to shatter, to fall through.
I have to break, to shatter, to fall through.

usagePhrases.note: 깨지다 = a hard/brittle thing shatters or cracks. The broken thing takes 이/가.

examples.en: The eggs broke inside my bag.
examples.note: For brittle things — 유리가/접시가/계란이 깨지다.

examples.en: The world record was broken.
examples.note: 기록이 깨지다 = a record gets broken; a fixed sports/news collocation.

examples.en: The mood was suddenly ruined.
examples.note: 분위기가 깨지다 = the vibe/mood breaks — when one comment spoils the moment.

화내다.en: to get angry, to lose one's temper

ex.ko: 참으려고 했는데 회의에서 결국 화를 내고 말았어요.
ex.en: I tried to hold back, but in the end I lost my temper in the meeting.
ex.note: 화를 내다 splits into 화 + 를 + 내다 inside a sentence.

화내다.nuance: 화내다 literally combines 화 (火, Sino-Korean 'fire' = anger) + 내다 ('to put out, let out'), so it pictures LETTING THE FIRE OUT — to OUTWARDLY SHOW or express anger (raising your voice, scolding). The essential contrast is with 화나다 (화 + 나다 'to arise'): 화나다 is the anger RISING inside you, an involuntary feeling ('I'm angry / I got mad', 화났어요), while 화내다 is the active VENTING of it toward someone ('he got angry at me', 나한테 화냈어요). So 화났어요 = 'I feel angry' (inner state), but 화냈어요 = 'I lashed out' (outward act). The target of 화내다 takes 한테/에게 (나한테 화내다), and the trigger takes 에 (작은 일에 화내다). Pitfall: English 'I'm angry' is the feeling — use 화났어요, NOT 화냈어요, which would mean you displayed anger at someone. Keep 내다 (let out) and 나다 (arise) straight; one letter flips agent vs experiencer.
화내다.explanation: "to get angry" in Korean is 화내다 (hwanaeda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 화내요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 화내다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 화내지 마세요 ("Please don't be angry") — then reshape the same stem into 화내고 싶어요 (desire), 화낼 수 있어요 (ability), and 화낼 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
화내다.shortExplanation: 화내다 means "to get angry" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 화내다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 화내요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 화냈어요 for 'I am/was angry' (the feeling). The feeling rising in you is 화나다 → 화났어요; 화내다 (화냈어요) means you actively vented anger at someone.
Marking the person you're mad at with 를: 너를 화내요. The target takes 한테/에게 — 너한테 화내요.
Confusing 내다 (let out) and 나다 (arise): 화내다 = show anger outward; 화나다 = anger wells up inside. Mixing the stems reverses who is doing what.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 화내다 becomes 화낼 수 있어요 ("can") and 화낼 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

examples.en: My father got angry
examples.note: Subject + 가 shows/expresses anger outwardly

examples.en: Please don't get angry at me
examples.note: 한테 = at/to me; the recipient of the anger

examples.en: He gets angry over small things
examples.note: 작은 일에 = at small matters; 에 marks the trigger

ex.en: I slipped on the stairs and nearly went down.
ex.note: The slip is real; only what follows it is the near miss.

미끄러지다.nuance: 미끄러지다 is the VERB 'to slip / slide / lose footing', describing the motion of your foot or body sliding on a slick surface. Its single most important confusion is with the look-alike ADJECTIVE 미끄럽다 ('to be slippery'): the surface IS 미끄럽다 (길이 미끄러워요 — a state, ㅂ-irregular), but a person DOES 미끄러지다 (제가 미끄러졌어요 — an event). Mixing the two is the number-one English-speaker error here. Keep it apart from 넘어지다 too: 미끄러지다 is the slide itself, 넘어지다 is hitting the ground, and they chain naturally — 미끄러져서 넘어졌어요. The slippery place takes 에서. Register is plain. Useful collocations: 발이 미끄러지다 (foot slips), 차가 미끄러지다 (a car skids), 미끄럼 주의 (the 'caution: slippery' floor sign, using the noun 미끄럼). The verb itself is regular (미끄러지다 → 미끄러져요), but its adjective cousin 미끄럽다 is ㅂ-irregular (미끄러워요), so don't carry the irregularity over.
미끄러지다.explanation: 미끄러지다 (mikkeureoji-da) = "to slip". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 미끄러져요 plus one useful sentence like 빙판에서 미끄러지다 ("to slip on the ice"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 미끄러지고 싶어요 for what you want, 미끄러질 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 미끄러져요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off.
미끄러지다.shortExplanation: 미끄러지다 means "to slip" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 미끄러지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 미끄러져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 길이 미끄러졌어요 to mean 'the road is slippery'. A road doesn't slip; it IS slippery — use the adjective: 길이 미끄러워요 (from 미끄럽다).
Conjugating the verb like the ㅂ-irregular adjective: 미끄러워요 for 'I slip'. The verb 미끄러지다 is regular: 미끄러져요. Save 미끄러워요 for the adjective 미끄럽다.
Using 미끄러지다 alone when you actually fell down. Slipping is the slide; if you ended up on the ground, add 넘어지다: 미끄러져서 넘어졌어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 미끄러지다 becomes 미끄러질 수 있어요 ("can") and 미끄러질 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Slippery surface takes 에서, where the slide happens

examples.en: I slipped on the floor.
examples.note: Simplest: surface 바닥 + 에서, past tense

examples.en: It rained so the road is slippery.
examples.note: Everyday contrast: here the ADJECTIVE 미끄럽다 'be slippery' describes the road

examples.en: I almost slipped on the stairs but grabbed the railing.
examples.note: Real situation: -ㄹ 뻔하다 'almost' + the rescue 난간을 잡다

후련하다.en: to feel relieved, to feel unburdened

ex.ko: 밀린 일을 다 끝내 버리니까 정말 후련해요.
ex.en: Now that I've finished off all the backlog, I feel genuinely unburdened.
ex.note: 후련하다 is the feeling that marks the relief reading of -아/어 버리다.

후련하다.nuance: 후련하다 names the clean, lightened sensation right after a burden or pent-up stress is released — finishing exams, finally venting, crying it out. Its near-synonym is 시원하다: 시원하다 is the broader word that also covers physical coolness (시원한 바람, a cool breeze) and refreshing drinks, while 후련하다 is reserved almost entirely for emotional/internal release, so '속이 후련하다' and '속이 시원하다' overlap but 바람이 후련하다 is wrong. It is NOT general happiness (기쁘다/행복하다) — it strictly presupposes something heavy was weighing on you and is now gone. As a 하다-adjective it conjugates 후련해요 / 후련했어요 / 후련해서, and it collocates above all with 속이, 가슴이, and the adverb 후련하게. English-speaker pitfall: learners reach for it as a synonym of 'happy', but if there was no preceding pressure to discharge, a Korean ear hears it as odd — 'I'm 후련해' out of plain good cheer sounds like a non sequitur.
후련하다.explanation: 후련하다 (huryeonhada) means "relieved (after a burden lifts); refreshed". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 후련해요 ("I feel relieved"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 후련하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
후련하다.shortExplanation: 후련하다 means "relieved (after a burden lifts); refreshed" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 후련하다 for plain happiness ('생일이라 후련해요') is wrong — it requires a preceding burden or stress that has just been lifted; for general joy use 기쁘다/행복하다.
Treating it as interchangeable with 시원하다 for physical coolness ('날씨가 후련해요') is wrong; 후련하다 is emotional/internal release only — say 시원하다 for a cool breeze or cold drink.
Saying '후련 있어요' (treating it like a noun) is wrong; it is an adjective, so conjugate it directly: 후련해요, 후련했어요.

usagePhrases.note: polite present; 하다-adjective, so 하 + 여요 contracts to 해요 — the most common spoken form

usagePhrases.en: to feel a weight off one's chest
usagePhrases.note: set phrase; literally 'the insides feel clear' — say this after venting or finishing something
adverb form (하다→하게), e.g. 후련하게 울다 to have a good cleansing cry
-아/어지다 attaches to the 해 stem and shows the shift from heavy to light

examples.en: I'm relieved the exam is over.
examples.note: simple 해요 form; use it when a stressful thing is done, not just when you're happy

examples.ko: 할 말을 다 하고 나니까 속이 후련하네요.
examples.romanization: hal mareul da hago nanikka sogi huryeonhaneyo.
examples.en: Now that I've said everything I wanted to, I feel so relieved.
examples.note: -고 나니까 'now that I've finished ~' frames the classic after-venting context

examples.ko: 몇 년 묵은 고민을 털어놓고 나니까 가슴이 다 후련하더라고요.
examples.romanization: myeon nyeon mugeun gomineul teoreonoko nanikka gaseumi da huryeonhadeoragoyo.
examples.en: After finally pouring out a worry I'd carried for years, my chest felt completely clear.
examples.note: real-situation; 다 here is intensifier 'completely', and -더라고요 reports the felt experience

들키다.en: to be caught out, to be found out

ex.en: I was pretending to be asleep, and in the end I got caught.
ex.note: 들키다 is itself a passive-shaped verb — you are the one found out.

ex.en: I very nearly lost my passport.
ex.note: Another lexicalized 버리다 verb; 잊어버리다 is for facts, 잃어버리다 for things.

실수하다.en: to make a mistake, to slip up

ex.ko: 안 그러려고 했는데 또 실수하고 말았어요.
ex.en: I meant not to, and I went and slipped up again.
ex.note: 안 그러려고 했는데 is the standard lead-in for a -고 말다 confession.

부딪히다.en: to bump into, to collide with

ex.en: The car in front braked hard, and I nearly hit it.
ex.note: 부딪히다 is the passive of 부딪다 — the collision happens to you.

숨기다.en: to hide (something), to keep something from someone

ex.ko: 숨기려고 했는데 표정에서 다 드러나 버렸어요.
ex.en: I meant to hide it, but my face gave the whole thing away.
ex.note: 숨기다 is the causative-shaped partner of 숨다 (to hide oneself).
